talks.title: Anatomy of a Cyber World | 2026 Kaspersky Security Services Global Report
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Anatomy of a Cyber World | 2026 Kaspersky Security Services Global Report.
talks.summary:
Overview: Kaspersky presents findings from its 2026 Security Services Global Report, highlighting MDR statistics and the gap between potential and actual breach detection.

Key Topics: More than two high-severity incidents detected daily via Kaspersky MDR; IT and government sectors leading in human-driven attacks; suspicious activity visible weeks before action; and compromise assessment as proactive threat hunting.

Technical Details: Two-thirds of incidents show suspicious activity hidden in endpoints and network traffic for weeks. Nearly 20% of 2025 incidents were discovered manually after bypassing automated controls, exposing blind spots in log-centric SOCs.

Takeaways: Automated controls alone miss sophisticated threats. Organizations need proactive compromise assessments and MDR to detect footholds before breaches materialize.

Security Services Structure

Alexander Zaytsev leads Kaspersky's Security Services Expertise Center, organizing work into offensive, defensive, and threat-intelligence streams. Together they provide a holistic view of customer security posture from both attacker and defender perspectives.

Lifecycle Service Portfolio

Services map to attack stages: Digital Footprint Intelligence and Brand Protection for reconnaissance, Security Assessment and penetration testing for simulated attacks, Compromise Assessment for hunting latent intrusions, Incident Response for containment, MDR for continuous monitoring, and SOC Consulting for operational maturity.

Offensive-Defensive Feedback Loop

Combining offensive and defensive expertise in one center creates a self-reinforcing system. Pentesters learn how SOC teams detect attacks, while defenders incorporate real attacker tradecraft from assessment findings.

Emerging Threat Trends

Zaytsev highlights trusted-relationship and supply-chain attacks where adversaries compromise low-security partners to reach larger targets via VPNs or stolen credentials. He also warns of increasingly destructive attacks where detection-to-impact windows can be minutes, demanding faster response processes.

talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for ICS CERT Expertise Center: Evgeny Goncharov on protecting the systems that run our world.
talks.summary:
OT Cybersecurity Scope

Kaspersky ICS CERT head Evgeny Goncharov defines operational technology security as protecting plants, transport, and smart infrastructure from attacks that stop production or cause physical harm—not just data theft.

Common Incident Patterns

Ransomware on IT systems often halts manufacturing because OT, logistics, and business networks are tightly coupled. A U.S. auto-dealer software supplier encryption incident cost clients over a billion dollars in three weeks.

Supply Chain and Regulations

Niche vendors with weak security become industry bottlenecks. Goncharov argues cybersecurity must be designed into cars, nuclear plants, and buildings early because retrofitting is impractical without strong regulation.

People and Emerging Tech

Industrial security blends IT security and engineering cultures. Kaspersky's ML anomaly detection on plant telemetry already flags attacks and operator mistakes, while IIoT and edge computing outpace current security tooling.

talks.title: Dmitry Shmoylov on building security from the ground up
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Threat Research Expertise Center: Dmitry Shmoylov on building security from the ground up.
talks.summary:
Role

Dmitry Shmoylov heads software security at Kaspersky, driving secure development lifecycle (SDLC/SSDLC) across products whose failures would be especially consequential given elevated privileges.

Investment and culture

Secure development can consume 15–20% of team capacity early and slows delivery, requiring involvement from developers through executives, security champions, standardized security gates, extensive tooling, and an active bug bounty program.

Challenges

High-privilege security products attract attackers; continuous control is essential. Checkbox security is insufficient—consistency release-to-release matters organization-wide.

Secure by design and cyberimmunity

Security must be architectural, not patchwork; KasperskyOS embeds controls at the OS level. Cyberimmunity balances security goals with business constraints so protections focus where exploitation cost to attackers is meaningful.

Lessons

Recent pentests and static-analysis gaps on optimized system code and widely used open-source libraries led to CVE filings and improved detection rules.

talks.title: Vladimir Kuskov on the threats that hide in plain sight
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Threat Research Expertise Center: Vladimir Kuskov on the threats that hide in plain sight.
talks.summary:
## SparkCat: App Store Stealer

Kaspersky Anti-Malware Research head Vladimir Kuskov discusses SparkCat, the first large-scale iOS stealer distributed through official app stores. Discovery began when Android Play Market monitoring flagged dynamically loaded code; cross-platform investigation found Rust-based apps using machine vision to scan photo galleries for cryptocurrency wallet recovery phrases.

## Evasion and Moderation Gaps

Apps posed as legitimate delivery and editing tools with real functionality plus hidden payloads. Heavy obfuscation and iOS research barriers made analysis difficult. Apple and Google removed apps after disclosure—rare for iOS, where malicious titles seldom reach consumers.

## Firmware and EDR Bypass Trends

Kuskov outlines UEFI threat scanning developed as bootkit samples proliferated, plus defenses against vulnerable-driver abuse that collapses kernel-user isolation. Attackers increasingly block EDR telemetry via firewall rules—legitimate OS capabilities repurposed—requiring vendors to harden self-protection across Windows versions.

## Threat Intelligence as Product

Kaspersky's ATT&CK-aligned intelligence portal lets customers filter by region, industry, and platform to prioritize detection rules. Unlike generic framework examples, Kaspersky supplies command-line samples, file hashes, and ready-made YARA-style guidance—aiming to replace manual parsing of thousands of annual threat reports for SOC tier-three analysts.

talks.title: How to detect a hidden camera
talks.teaser: Explains practical ways to spot hidden cameras using lens glare, smartphones, dedicated detectors and Wi-Fi scanning apps.
talks.summary:
Hidden cameras and microphones turn up in rented flats, hotel rooms, offices, saunas and private homes. The video frames the risk as covert filming for extortion, pranks or landlord snooping, and lays out four ways to check a space: hiring a professional sweep, using dedicated or improvised detectors, using a smartphone, and using dedicated software.

The optical method depends on lens reflection. A light source placed close to the viewer's eye makes a camera lens appear as a bright dot, the same effect that makes reflectors and cat's-eye road studs glow. A homemade detector needs an LED and, optionally, a filter, and its range is only a few meters, so a full sweep is slow. Because hidden lenses are tiny, the speaker suggests checking the bathroom and bedroom first, then objects that have a clear view of the room, such as smoke detectors, appliances, paintings, clocks, flowerpots and toys. A smartphone can work in a similar way, using its flashlight and camera to show glare, or its sensitivity to infrared, which reveals the night-vision light of a camera when a TV remote is pointed at the phone. These phone checks suit only a quick look.

Software falls into two groups: apps that find lens glare and apps that scan for connected devices on Wi-Fi. One Wi-Fi app, Lumos, was described as showing device locations in augmented reality, though it is still in development. Wi-Fi scanners are weak in smart homes or networks with many connected devices. The takeaway is that these low-cost methods can catch some covert cameras, but none is thorough, so a professional check is worth considering for a long-term new home.

talks.title: OS: areas of application and development plans
talks.teaser: Explains how KasperskyOS differs from other microkernel systems and how it is moving into general-purpose devices.
talks.summary:
In this interview, Andrey Nenko, development team manager for KasperskyOS, discusses where the operating system sits among microkernel-based systems and where its development is heading. The conversation opens with the point that cyber immune principles apply regardless of platform, while KasperskyOS provides architectural support for them out of the box.

Nenko explains that the project combines established techniques instead of inventing everything from scratch. It uses object capabilities, a model also found in designs such as seL4, together with a reference monitor called the Kaspersky Security Monitor, an older idea that few operating systems implement. Pairing the two lets developers bring communications under control in ways that are hard to achieve on other systems. He presents the platform as a set of building blocks for designing secure solutions from a threat model and analysis, rather than treating security as an abstract property.

The discussion then turns to the shift from the original focus on specialized, niche embedded devices, where process connections are fixed at boot, toward general-purpose devices with dynamic behavior. Smartphone-style systems must download, verify, launch and terminate applications and manage their lifecycles, which creates new problems the team has to solve. Nenko frames these challenges as the main driver for the platform's next stage of development.

talks.title: Decoding Crypto Mining: Legit vs. Scam
talks.teaser: Explains how fake GPU sales, malicious miners and cryptojacking target people buying into crypto mining, and how to avoid them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the rise in cryptocurrency prices and the scarcity of powerful graphics cards used for mining, which has made mining hardware an attractive lure for fraudsters. It describes a recent scam, identified by Kaspersky, in which criminals sell fake high-end video cards through cloned vendor websites. Victims are reached through email, social media or document-sharing notifications, and are pressed to pay only in cryptocurrency within a two-hour window, after which the money is gone.

The presenter then outlines several other schemes. Malicious mining software or apps send the mined coins to a criminal's wallet instead of the user's. Cryptojacking installs a miner on a device without the owner noticing and consumes its processing power. A third variant is a fake mining app built to steal personal data or wallet credentials.

To avoid these scams, viewers are advised to slow down when pressured to pay, be wary of suddenly available scarce products, check the official vendor site and its address bar when an offer comes from a known brand, and research any mining deal that looks too good to be true. They should also download mining software only from reliable sources and use a security product that detects known and unknown crypto scams, including cryptojacking. The closing point is that anonymous, irreversible transactions make crypto an easy target, so payments should wait until safety is certain.

talks.title: What is crypto phishing?
talks.teaser: Explains what crypto phishing is, how scammers lure victims to fake sites, and simple steps to protect wallets and logins.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces crypto phishing as a scam type that has become as common in cryptocurrency as it has long been in general online fraud. It cites US Federal Trade Commission figures showing that 46,000 people reported losses of over a billion dollars in crypto to scams between January 2021 and March 2022.

Attackers typically reach victims by email, text or social media, impersonating a familiar brand, a bank or a government body. Their messages play on urgency, a sense of opportunity or fear, such as a claimed prize or a supposed threat to savings. The link leads to a counterfeit site that resembles a real one but contains subtle differences, such as a slightly altered web address. Anyone who enters login details or a wallet's private key hands over control of their funds. Kaspersky's anti-phishing system reported more than five million fraudulent resources in 2022 aimed at crypto investors and miners, a 40 percent rise over 2021.

The practical defenses covered are straightforward. Do not click links in unexpected messages, and verify the sender through a separate, independent channel. Never share account details or private keys, since legitimate transactions never require them. Bookmark trusted crypto sites and visit only through those bookmarks. Use strong, unique passwords with two-factor authentication, and consider a password manager and a comprehensive security product. The talk closes by warning that these scams are likely to grow as cryptocurrency becomes more mainstream, and that careful habits can keep funds safe.

talks.title: What to do if you lose your smartphone: protecting data and accounts
talks.teaser: Walks through the steps to take right after a phone is lost or stolen, from blocking the SIM to wiping data remotely.
talks.summary:
The video covers what to do when a smartphone is lost or stolen and the owner was not prepared in advance. It starts with urgent steps that require a borrowed phone: calling the mobile operator to block the SIM so a thief cannot receive verification codes, then alerting family and friends so they can warn contacts about possible scam messages or requests for money.

Next, the presenter recommends locking the device from a trusted computer rather than a public one. Viewers are advised to use the backup codes saved when two-factor authentication was set up, sign in to the Google or Apple ID account, and use the device-finding service to mark the phone as lost or secure it with a lock-screen message and a callback number. On Android, the wipe option is also mentioned, with the caveat that tracking stops afterward and an SD card may keep data. Bank cards should be removed from the payment settings of the account rather than blocked with the bank, since only the phone is gone. In countries such as the US, UK and Latvia, the IMEI can be reported to the carrier so the handset cannot register on networks.

The remaining steps are reporting the theft to police, changing passwords for apps and browser-saved logins, re-enabling two-factor authentication on the new phone, and restoring data from a backup. The video closes by urging preparation in advance, such as enabling backups and screen locking, and reminds viewers that personal safety matters most.

Other prompts cover reviewing privacy settings, reporting hateful comments instead of replying to trolls, keeping social media logins to themselves, and not leaving a phone with others, even friends. The questions are framed as a game in which each correct answer moves a participant forward.

A second segment is a short interview with two Emirati motorsport drivers, Amna and Hamda Al Qubaisi, tied to a Kaspersky book in which a character named Lola learns that girls can become racing drivers. They describe how they came into karting and motorsport, with one crediting her father and the other her sister, and how they handled being among very few women in a male-dominated field. Their stated goals include becoming the first Emirati woman to race in Formula One.

The closing part covers smartphone habits. Screen time limits for teenagers, whether phone use affects real-world connection, and the value of putting a phone away during time with others are discussed in short answers. One interviewee says she checks any link from an unknown number before clicking it, and uses a Kaspersky app to verify whether a website is safe.

talks.title: It started with innocent pranks. Now he faces life in prison
talks.teaser: Follows how the RaidForums hacking forum grew out of teenage Twitch pranks, and the debate over prosecuting young offenders.
talks.summary:
The segment looks at RaidForums, an underground hacking forum that grew out of Twitch raiding. Its founder, who goes by Omnipotent, reportedly started it at 14 as a platform for coordinated raids that pranked streamers. The pranks escalated into bullying and bomb threats, then into leaking stolen databases. Once the data proved valuable, the forum began selling it and acting as an escrow middleman for criminal deals, earning millions.

Security journalist Waqas recounts how the FBI reportedly knew the founder's identity for years. When he visited the United States as a minor, his devices were seized but he was not arrested. Investigators reportedly let the forum keep running to gather information on buyers and sellers before it was seized, and its database is now held by the FBI. An extradition lawyer explains that US prosecutors typically count from adulthood, which can mean de facto life sentences, even for conduct committed as a minor.

Other contributors look at why young people end up in this world. A psychologist says many are socially isolated and find belonging in hacker communities, where peers may encourage them to monetise their skills. The segment also notes that defendants are often diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, and recalls the case of Laurie Love, who was discharged on mental health grounds. The piece closes with the argument that children should be held accountable without facing the same consequences as adults.

talks.title: What is Social Engineering?
talks.teaser: Explains how social engineering exploits fear, urgency and trust to push people into risky actions.
talks.summary:
This short explainer opens with a familiar scam: a text warning that a debit card was used for a fraudulent purchase and demanding a quick reply. The speaker explains that social engineering is a manipulation technique in which criminals trick people into revealing passwords or card details, clicking a malicious link, or opening an attachment or app that spreads malware. In some cases attackers try to use an employee to reach restricted systems. The goal is usually theft of money or information, or sabotage of a business through disrupted or corrupted data.

The middle of the talk describes three traits that these attacks rely on. The first is heightened emotion, since fear or anger from a threatening message, or excitement and curiosity from a prize pop-up, makes people more likely to take risky steps. The second is urgency, where a demand to act immediately is meant to override careful thinking. The third is trust, where attackers copy brand logos and websites, and the difference often shows up as a slightly altered site name or low-quality images. The speaker lists the channels involved, including email, text, automated voice messages, DNS spoofing that redirects browsers to malicious sites, and scareware with false infection warnings. Physical intrusion is also covered, with impostors posing as employees or vendors, or someone asking a person to hold a restricted door open.

The closing section offers a short checklist to run when a message feels suspicious: whether emotions are running high, whether the sender is legitimate or uses lookalike characters, whether the URL, images or wording look off, whether an offer seems too good to be true, whether a file name is vague, and whether the person can actually prove who they are. The practical advice is to slow down when a message creates pressure and to avoid sharing sensitive information in response to it.

talks.title: What is Netiquette?
talks.teaser: Explains netiquette, the etiquette expected online, and lists twelve guidelines for respectful communication.
talks.summary:
This short video introduces netiquette, the idea of applying traditional etiquette to online communication. It explains that connecting through a keyboard with a degree of anonymity makes people more likely to forget their manners, and that many websites, forums and social platforms set their own conduct rules and use moderators to remove those who break them.

The core of the piece is a list of twelve guidelines. They cover treating people online as you would in person, thinking before posting because screenshots can outlast a deleted post, and staying calm and respectful when you disagree. Other points advise reading a full thread before asking or answering, proofreading messages for clarity, and keeping replies brief. Privacy advice includes using the blind carbon copy field for group emails, asking permission before sharing or forwarding other people's photos or information, and not entering someone else's details when signing up for services. The list also warns administrators not to misuse private data they can reach, urges people to leave flame wars rather than trade insults, and suggests learning the norms of an unfamiliar community before joining in. It ends by encouraging users to report hate speech.

The closing message is that good netiquette is appreciated and that polite behavior online is a smart habit. The video finishes by pointing viewers to links for Kaspersky's products that help them stay safe online.

talks.title: What Is Cyberstalking and How To Prevent It
talks.teaser: Explains what cyberstalking is and gives practical steps to limit online exposure and respond to harassment.
talks.summary:
The video defines cyberstalking as using electronic communication to intimidate or harass someone, and notes that both men and women can be victims or perpetrators. It lists common tactics: trolling, threatening messages, hacked email, spreading lies to a victim's friends, family and employer, posting or threatening revenge porn, tracking through social media activity, spyware on phones, and GPS devices attached to vehicles. It also describes catfishing, where a fake relationship is used to obtain intimate images for blackmail or to request money in a fake emergency. The video notes that US state and federal laws, and UK law, allow offenders to be fined or imprisoned.

Prevention starts with searching your own name to see which personal details, such as phone numbers and addresses, are publicly visible, including on friends' and family members' profiles. The next step is removing that data from websites, tightening privacy settings, hiding optional profile fields, limiting posts to trusted contacts, turning off location features, and logging out of social media. On devices, the video recommends avoiding public Wi-Fi without a VPN, installing anti-spyware, using a hard-to-guess password, blocking the stalker's number, and allowing GPS and contact access only for apps that need it.

For existing victims, the video advises warning the stalker in writing to stop contacting you, then ceasing all communication and going to the police if the behavior continues. A professional can check devices for spyware, and every incident should be reported to the social network and, for threatening work contact, to the employer. Abusive email senders can be blocked and reported to their internet provider. The video closes by urging victims to save emails, texts, posts, screenshots and photos, backed up on a separate drive, to support police reports.

talks.title: How to Protect Yourself Against Cybercrime
talks.teaser: Lists seven everyday habits, from software updates to password managers, that help people avoid becoming victims of cybercrime.
talks.summary:
This short awareness video explains how ordinary people can avoid becoming victims of cybercrime. It notes that criminals usually aim to steal money, and that personal data stays out of reach when devices are properly secured and users recognise common tactics. The presenter then walks through seven practical habits.

The first habits focus on basic technical hygiene. Installing operating system and software updates delivers security patches and bug fixes, and antivirus software can scan, detect and remove threats, so it should be kept current too. Strong, unique passwords are recommended, ideally generated and stored by a password manager. The video then explains common threats, including Trojans, phishing, ransomware, DDoS attacks and data breaches, and advises against opening attachments or clicking links from unknown senders.

Further advice covers social engineering and online money. Personal details should not be given over the phone or by email; instead, the caller should hang up and dial the official number from the company's website, preferably from a different phone. Viewers should check a URL before clicking, especially on ads, and make online purchases only through secure sites. Checking bank statements for unfamiliar activity completes the list. The video ends with a promotion for a Kaspersky security product.

talks.title: What is Cryptocurrency?
talks.teaser: Explains what cryptocurrency is, how blockchains and mining work, and how to start investing and stay safe.
talks.summary:
The video opens by defining cryptocurrency as a currency that exists purely online, secured with encryption and bought from brokers and kept in digital wallets. Unlike conventional banking, it is not tied to a central bank or overseen by a single regulator, and people can send value directly to one another. Every transaction is recorded on a decentralized public ledger made of linked blocks, known as a blockchain.

It then covers how new coins enter circulation through mining, where computers solve complex mathematical problems and receive currency in return. Mining demands heavy processing power and electricity, which is why some companies reward miners for their computing resources. The presenter stresses that owning crypto means holding a digital key rather than a physical asset, and that trading carries real risk because of price volatility and limited regulation. A short beginner's path follows: choose an exchange or online broker, fund the account with ordinary money or a payment service, and move the coins into a wallet. Spending crypto is harder, since few retailers accept it, although some luxury stores, car dealers, and crypto debit cards can help.

On safety, the video argues that blockchain technology and two-factor checks make transactions difficult to tamper with, so criminals tend to target exchanges rather than personal wallets. Frauds remain common, including counterfeit sites, phony trading platforms, fake celebrity endorsements, and romance-based cons. The main takeaway for a newcomer is to verify any platform or offer carefully before sending money.

Securing them means protecting the orchestration and runtime infrastructure as well as the containers themselves, including checking the images they are built from.

The speaker lists the problems customers face. Container infrastructure is complex and varied. Images from contractors, partners or public sources may carry vulnerabilities or malware. Orchestration platforms can be misconfigured, operating system images and software can contain errors, and compliance with regulations can lapse. Compromised containers can also threaten the platform they run on. The planned product is meant to address these areas and give users visibility into how their container infrastructure works, with current data on security risks.

Kaspersky says the product will offer a complete feature set for this kind of solution, with some features leading the market, such as updating databases and policies in real time. The broader strategy is to extend its XDR platform to cover all digital asset scenarios for corporate customers, and the company aims to be the first XDR vendor to add container security. talks.title: What is Cyber Immunity?
talks.teaser: Presents Cyber Immunity, an architecture approach that isolates components and controls interactions so attacks become impractical.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with the spread of Internet of Things devices, now numbering over twelve billion, many of them cheap and weakly protected, including industrial and medical equipment. It points out that a compromised gateway at a factory could reach the systems that control production, and cites a 2022 attack on a steel mill unit supplying hot metal that failed and caused a severe fire. The speaker argues that patching known flaws and detecting threats is not enough against these risks.

Cyber Immunity is introduced as an alternative that assumes anything hackable will eventually be hacked. Instead of trying to remove every vulnerability, the aim is an architecture that makes exploiting flaws too costly to be worthwhile. The approach rests on four principles: isolating components into separate security domains, using a security monitor that passes only whitelisted interactions between them, keeping code minimal through a microkernel operating system with far fewer lines of code than a monolithic kernel, and running a security development process that defines required tasks before the architecture is designed.

The talk closes with examples of existing products, including IoT gateways that connect operational technology environments with IT networks, and a thin client meant to secure the last mile of virtual desktop infrastructure. The main takeaway is that security should be judged against the specific tasks a device must perform under attack, rather than against an impossible goal of total invulnerability.

talks.title: What Advanced Threat Actors Got Up to in Q3 2022
talks.teaser: Kaspersky researchers survey Q3 2022 APT activity, covering the Dtrack, Metatron and DiceF campaigns.
talks.summary:
This Kaspersky overview covers advanced persistent threat activity during the third quarter of 2022. The presenters, from the company's research team, explain that some groups keep their tooling steady while others refresh it and widen their campaigns.

The first case is Dtrack, a backdoor used by the Lazarus Group that has surfaced in ATM breaches, a nuclear power plant and, more recently, Europe. Its core functions changed little, but the authors added an obfuscation layer and slightly altered standard encryption routines. Metatron is a previously unknown set of Windows tools, including the intermediate backdoor Metamain and the modular implant Mafalda, which run in memory and are launched by abusing a legitimate program. It is highly evasive and was linked by a partner vendor to an actor called Metador, which targeted telecom firms and academic institutions across the Middle East and Africa. Its infrastructure is never reused, and no attribution has been made.

The third case is DiceF, which targets online casinos in Southeast Asia. The researchers suspect the actors want the players, customers and flow of money rather than cash itself, since they quietly monitored developers, contractors and network staff without moving funds. The talk ends with advice to give security operations teams current threat intelligence, upskill staff, and use enterprise EDR tools.

talks.summary:
This Kaspersky video gathers insights from three managers working in different parts of the company on what makes a good leader. They explain that leadership means less hands-on technical work and more communication, listening and asking questions, since people often do not say what they mean. One manager, who leads technology scouting for a product studio, stresses that scouts need intuition as well as technical skill to choose projects that fit the portfolio.

Their career examples show the range of work involved. One describes a parental-control education project for parents, teachers and children, and a healthcare campaign that brought together communications, social media, sales and marketing. Another describes an anti-stalkerware initiative, run with NGOs and industry partners, that teaches people how to find and remove spyware and prevent it being installed on their phone. A third admits an early mistake: trying to please everyone, and not following up when a journalist went silent after an interview, which later led to negative coverage.

For feedback, they advise starting with something positive, keeping emotion out, and framing criticism around a function rather than a person. Leaders should also build an atmosphere where their team feels able to give them feedback. When stuck, they turn to colleagues inside the company or to supportive industry communities. The video closes with hobbies such as diving, board games and sports, which the managers say build humility, focus and motivation.

talks.title: What Advanced Threat Actors Got Up to in the first half of 2022
talks.teaser: Summarizes a review of advanced persistent threat activity in the first half of 2022, from wartime wipers to firmware implants.
talks.summary:
The talk reviews how advanced persistent threat groups changed their activity in the first half of 2022. The presenters tie much of that activity to the conflict in Ukraine, which brought new infrastructure, a run of destructive wipers and disinformation campaigns. Overlapping operations and leaked corporate data made attribution harder.

Firmware-level threats came next. The MoonBounce UEFI implant was attributed to APT41, while CosmicStrength, a boot kit that targets only certain motherboards, was linked to a previously unknown Chinese-speaking actor. In cryptocurrency, a trojan hidden inside a wallet application shared tools with a known group, and a campaign aimed at South Korean investors used malicious macros in documents. The IIS backdoors, modules for Microsoft's web server often deployed after Exchange ProxyLogon exploitation, were found in six variants and used mainly for espionage.

The presenters closed with defensive advice: stay vigilant, give security teams current threat intelligence, build staff skills, deploy EDR and network tools that spot targeted attacks early, and run awareness training, since many such attacks begin with phishing. They stressed that APT campaigns are rarely one-off, so organizations should stay alert continuously.

talks.title: A new phishing technique: browser-in-the-browser attack
talks.teaser: Explains how fake login windows drawn inside a web page can harvest credentials, and how to spot them.
talks.summary:
The video introduces "browser-in-the-browser" phishing, a scheme described by researcher mr.d0x. Common advice says to check the domain name in the address bar, but this technique defeats that check by drawing a convincing login window inside the page itself. The example is a job board for young mothers that offers sign-in through Facebook, Google or Apple so visitors can skip registration.

When a visitor picks a social login, the window that appears is only an image on the phishing page, not a separate browser window. Credentials typed into it go to the attackers' server rather than to the identity provider. The key tell is that real authentication windows can be dragged beyond the edge of the browser, while the fake one stays confined to the boundaries of the page it sits on.

Not everyone will run that check every time, so the video points to security software. A password manager can refuse to fill credentials on a site whose URL does not match a known service, and an anti-phishing module checks addresses and warns about dangerous ones. Two-factor authentication is the final safeguard, since stolen passwords alone cannot open an account without a one-time code sent to the owner.

talks.title: What’s wrong with free public Wi-Fi
talks.teaser: Explains why public Wi-Fi is risky and how a personal hotspot or VPN keeps your data encrypted.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with a common habit: connecting to free public Wi-Fi in cafes, airports, trains, and parks. Public networks often skip encryption, so anyone on the same network can read traffic such as emails, passwords and card details. An attacker can also set up a fake access point with a convincing name, and phones that join known networks automatically may connect to it without the user noticing. The speaker notes that hotel and rented apartment networks carry similar risks, since attackers may target guest data and the network owner could monitor traffic.

Two protective options are presented. The first is to avoid untrusted networks by using a smartphone's own hotspot, provided encryption is enabled and a strong password is set. From a security standpoint it is as safe as a home router, though mobile data costs can be high when roaming abroad. The second is a virtual private network, which encrypts traffic so that card numbers and passwords stay protected even on an open network.

The speaker illustrates VPN use with a Kaspersky Secure Connection example. The app turns on the VPN with one tap, checks the networks it joins and warns about risky ones, and can be set to activate automatically on known public networks or when specific programs handle confidential data. The main takeaway is that a practitioner should either avoid open networks or make sure traffic is encrypted before sending sensitive information.

talks.title: Explaining blockchain, cryptocurrency and NFT in a one-dollar bill example
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Explaining blockchain, cryptocurrency and NFT in a one-dollar bill example.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this discussion, Ivan Imhoff breaks down the fundamental concepts behind blockchain, cryptocurrency, and non-fungible tokens (NFTs) using relatable analogies such as a one-dollar bill. The conversation explores the roots of Web3, contrasting traditional trust-based systems with decentralized, trustless environments, and reviews market volatility cycles as well as emerging utilitarian use cases for digital tokens.

### Key Topics
- **Understanding Blockchain:** Described as a sequential digital accounting ledger where validated transactions link back to all preceding transactions, creating an immutable, irreversible, and uneraseable record.
- **Trustless Systems vs. Traditional Trust:** Traditional finance, tech platforms, and art ownership require trusting intermediaries like banks, governments, Google, or Facebook. In contrast, blockchain operates in a trustless environment where verification occurs automatically without relying on third parties.
- **Fungibility and NFTs:** Standard currency and crypto tokens are fungible (like exchanging standard one-dollar bills). In contrast, an NFT is a non-fungible token representing a unique identifier on the blockchain, comparable to drawing a unique design onto a specific dollar bill so it can no longer be interchanged.
- **The Evolution of NFTs:** While initial adoption centered on hype, scarcity, art, and collectibles (such as CryptoPunks and Bored Ape Yacht Club), the sector is moving toward utilitarian value. Practical applications include event ticketing/registration, community access, and automated royalty distributions directly programmed for creators like musicians.
- **Market Cycles and Volatility:** Historical crypto market patterns feature dramatic bull and bear cycles roughly every three to four years, often pegged to Bitcoin halving phases and driven by human emotion and hype.

### Technical Details
- **Ledger Structure:** Each piece of the blockchain represents a batch of transactions validated at once, chained sequentially to all previous transactions back to origin.
- **Immutability:** Once transactions are validated on the ledger, they cannot be erased, altered, or reversed.
- **Programmed Royalties:** NFTs allow logic to be embedded directly into tokens, enabling automated revenue distribution (e.g., compensating an artist each time a song is played) without central entities like record labels.
- **Asset Classification:** Cryptocurrencies and NFTs behave as risk-on tech assets subject to extreme volatility, with drawdowns of 95% or more following major bull runs.

### Takeaways
- **Value in Bear Markets:** Correction periods—which may last from six months to two years—provide the best opportunity to build, learn, code, and identify enduring projects after speculative excess is flushed out.
- **Utility Over Hype:** Long-term sustainability for NFTs relies on shifting from pure collectibles and speculative art to real-world utility such as access, licensing, and automated revenue sharing.
- **Market Psychology:** Understanding recurring multi-year cycle dynamics helps navigate fear, euphoria, and extreme volatility without succumbing to emotional decision-making.

talks.title: Data leaks and when to change your password
talks.teaser: Explains how data leaks expose accounts even with strong passwords, and when a password change is needed.
talks.summary:
Strong passwords do not protect an account when the online service holding it is breached. The talk points to large incidents, including a 2013 breach that reportedly exposed more than two billion Yahoo mail accounts, and leaks affecting LinkedIn and Dropbox. Stolen records often surface for sale later, and the affected company may not notice right away. Criminals sometimes wait for years, quietly watching how an account is used for material they could sell or use for blackmail or phishing. They may also abuse the account to spread malware or spam, which does not require changing the login.

Leaks can be spotted in several ways. Take emails from well-known services about incidents and password resets seriously, and open the site by typing its address yourself rather than following a link, since scammers imitate these notices to harvest current passwords. Some services delay telling users or try to hide breaches. Security experts also post about credentials offered for sale, but their posts are often jargon-heavy and mostly irrelevant to any one person. The talk then presents a notification service in Kaspersky Security Cloud that monitors leaks and alerts only users whose data is affected, explaining in plain terms what happened, the risk, and the steps to take.

The talk closes by recommending two-factor authentication where it is available, since it makes things harder for someone who has obtained a username and password. Combined with strong passwords and prompt changes after a leak, these measures keep attackers away from private information. The talk then turns to how much personal information you reveal yourself.

talks.title: How to protect your accounts
talks.teaser: Explains how to build strong, unique passwords and why reuse, sharing and password managers matter for account safety.
talks.summary:
This short clip opens with the risk that criminals target online accounts by guessing or stealing passwords. It lists common mistakes: short or predictable strings such as simple numbers or the word "password", and details that can be pulled from a social network, like a pet's name or a spouse's birthday. Reusing one password across several services is flagged as especially dangerous, because a leak from one weakly protected site lets attackers try the same username and password elsewhere. Sharing passwords with friends, family or colleagues is also discouraged.

The clip defines a strong password as at least 10 characters, with 15 recommended for the most important accounts. It should be random or non-obvious to an outsider and mix upper and lower case letters, numbers and symbols. To make such passwords memorable, it suggests building one from the first letters of a favorite song, poem or other text you know well, then adding a symbol and a digit, plus a character tied to the site, such as its first letter or main color. Viewers are encouraged to devise their own scheme so each account gets a unique password.

For those who find this impractical, a password manager is presented as an alternative. It generates robust passwords, stores them, and requires only one master password to be remembered. The clip warns that attackers may still try to steal credentials through phishing or spyware, and it points to a security course for more detail. It closes by noting that credentials can also be taken directly from the service that holds them, so users cannot rely on passwords alone.

talks.title: How Fakecalls pretends to be a bank employee
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning How Fakecalls pretends to be a bank employee.
talks.summary:
Fakecalls is a sophisticated Korean Trojan malware targeting customers of Korean banks, specifically mimicking apps from Kookmin Bank and KakaoBank. The malware displays authentic bank support phone numbers harvested from official websites to appear legitimate.

The attack mechanism is elegant: when a user calls their bank's official hotline, Fakecalls detects the outgoing call, silently terminates the connection, and displays a fake call screen. The victim, unaware of the interception, is then routed to attackers posing as bank employees. The Trojan requests extensive permissions including access to contacts, microphone, camera, geolocation, and call control—typical for banking trojans but particularly dangerous in this context.

After intercepting a call, Fakecalls operates in two possible modes. It can directly connect the victim to human scammers disguised as bank support staff, or it can take control of the conversation itself using AI-generated voice responses. Currently, the voice imitation is limited to standard phrases in Korean typical of answering machines and call-center employees. The attackers exploit the false trust created by the victim initiating the contact, using social engineering to extract sensitive information such as payment data, login credentials, CVV codes, and verification codes.

A key vulnerability is the language mismatch: if the phone's interface is in English but suddenly displays a Korean call screen, users may detect the deception. However, for Korean-language users, this red flag disappears.

Kaspersky detects the threat as 'Trojan-Banker.AndroidOS.Fakecalls.' Recommended defenses include: download apps only from official app stores where security scanning occurs; carefully review and deny unnecessary permissions, especially for calls and messages; never disclose personal or financial information over the phone; verify suspicious calls by hanging up and contacting the bank directly via their official website; and install reputable cybersecurity solutions.

talks.title: Save the Coin: BlueNoroff
talks.teaser: Explains how the BlueNoroff APT group targets crypto startups with fake venture firm lures and tampered wallet extensions.
talks.summary:
Kaspersky's short video profiles BlueNoroff, an APT actor that abuses cryptocurrency startups to drain their accounts. The group first studies successful startups to learn what they care about, then runs social engineering that looks like ordinary exchanges between co-workers or partners. Researchers reported finding more than 15 venture firms whose brand or staff names were misused during the Snatch Crypto campaign.

The campaign's lure is a business-looking file, often posing as contracts from venture capital firms, which is really a macro-enabled document carrying a full-featured backdoor. Once a victim opens it, the operators can watch them for weeks or even months. A separate tactic targets people who manage crypto wallets through popular browser extensions such as MetaMask. The attackers swap the core of the legitimate extension for a tampered version that rewrites the recipient address on transfers and maxes out the amount, emptying the account in one move. The speaker says the group has already hit startups in the USA, China, India and other regions.

The closing advice is to keep browser and wallet protections switched on and heed any scam-site warning, since crypto attacks rely on social engineering much like traditional scams. Be cautious about offers promising profitable coin sales, and treat unexpected business files with suspicion even when they appear to come from known partners.

talks.title: How to block cookies in your browser the right way
talks.teaser: Shows how to block third-party cookies in Chrome, Safari, Firefox and Edge, with a short history of cookies.
talks.summary:
The video opens with a short history of the term "cookie," which traces back to small data files that programs exchanged, and notes that browser cookies arrived on the web in 1994. It then explains that websites store a small file on a visitor's device. Basic cookies personalize a site, such as remembering a chosen city or language or keeping a user logged in. Third-party cookies gather information for targeted advertising and analytics, which is why many people choose to block them.

The main part is a step-by-step walkthrough of blocking third-party cookies in each browser. In Chrome, the viewer opens the Security and privacy settings, selects the option to block third-party cookies, and can add per-site exceptions under customized behaviors. Safari already blocks third-party cookies by default, but the presenter recommends confirming that cross-site tracking prevention is on and reviewing stored site data under Manage Website Data. Firefox offers Standard, Strict and Custom protection levels; the presenter favors Custom, where all third-party cookies can be blocked and specific sites can be allowed or blocked through the exceptions list. In Edge, the setting is found under Cookies and site permissions.

The video closes by noting that blocking third-party cookies protects privacy while most favorite websites keep working. It points viewers to linked articles for the harder choices, such as whether to block all cookies or only some, and whether to delete them manually or automatically.

talks.title: Why do cybercriminals want your computer?
talks.teaser: Explains how criminals use infected computers for hidden crypto mining, spam, and botnet attacks, and what owners can do.
talks.summary:
This lesson asks why criminals would bother with a victim's computer when plain theft is an option. Its answer is that the device itself can be worth more to attackers than its contents, because an infected machine can be put to work earning money without its owner noticing.

The first case covered is hidden cryptocurrency mining. Malicious miners run quietly in the background, using the machine's processing power to generate digital coins for the attacker. The infected computer draws large amounts of electricity, slows down, and runs very hot, which can eventually damage the hardware. The lesson notes that the overheating risk is even greater on a smartphone. The second case is botnets, networks of infected machines that malware turns into bots under a remote operator's control. A single computer earns little, but thousands of them can send spam or malware, download illegal content, try to guess passwords for other accounts, or flood a company's website with requests until real users cannot reach it.

The owner of a compromised machine typically becomes an unwitting accomplice in these schemes. The lesson's practical advice is ordinary vigilance: install anti-virus software on every device and follow basic security habits to keep the computer out of criminal hands.

talks.title: 5 minutes with a reverse engineer ー Ivan Kwiatkowski
talks.teaser: A Kaspersky GReAT reverse engineer shares how he entered the field, what drives his work, and how he learns.
talks.summary:
## Overview

This interview features Ivan Kwiatkowski, a senior security researcher at Kaspersky's GReAT team, discussing his specialization in reverse engineering and his journey in cybersecurity. The interviewer, Liza, explores how he entered the field, what aspects he finds most engaging, and offers insights for aspiring security professionals.

## How He Entered Cybersecurity

Ivan began his cybersecurity career at age 19 while studying general computer science. He developed an interest in Wi-Fi security, took online classes, and never left the field. He emphasizes that his early introduction and consistent engagement set the foundation for his career.

## Reverse Engineering Focus

Although he initially thought offensive penetration testing would be his preferred specialization, Ivan discovered his passion for reverse engineering—reading and understanding malware code. He explains his preference by noting that unlike penetration testing, where success is uncertain, reverse engineering through persistent effort always yields results. This certainty of eventual success through hard work is what he values most.

## Challenges and Rewards

The most challenging aspect of the job is maintaining persistence. Hours spent analyzing seemingly meaningless instructions and CPU operations can be mentally draining and feels "against nature." However, the satisfaction comes from eventual success after sustained effort—a feeling that drives him forward despite the difficulty.

## Notable Discovery

Ivan's proudest achievement was connecting new traces of malicious activity called "Tomiris" to the existing SolarWinds incident. This discovery was significant because it identified previously unnoticed connections to a major case that impacted the world.

## Career Advice

He recommends newcomers only pursue cybersecurity if they are genuinely passionate, as the learning curve is steep and requires substantial personal commitment. Success requires doing what you love and persisting until you achieve your goals.

## Learning Preferences and Tools

Regarding learning methods, Ivan has evolved from using videos to preferring books and articles for their efficiency in accessing specific knowledge. Regarding tools, he mentions that while he long relied on Iproat, recent developments in Ghidra (an open-source alternative) suggest a viable transition path.

## Culture and Practical Insights

On naming malware or APT groups, he prefers clever or funny names over formal conventions. For media recommendations, he cites Mr. Robot (seasons 1–5) as uniquely accurate in technical representation. He also highlights an effective but seemingly counterintuitive protective measure: regularly rebooting phones can remove sophisticated malware that does not persist across reboots.

talks.title: What are the similarities between developing Diablo III and mobile cybersecurity quest?
talks.teaser: Uses the Diablo III development story to draw lessons on deadlines and scope cuts in product releases.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the familiar pressure of shipping a long-awaited game, when a build is ready but the team weighs postponing it to rework parts of it. The speaker draws on the book Blood, Sweat, and Pixels, arguing that developers of small indie titles and large blockbuster franchises run into the same problems.

Using Diablo III as the main case, the speaker says the game shipped nearly two years later than planned. The speaker's own team also released its game close to a year late. The core problem described is that the initial concept and the final product can turn out to be very different games, because ambitions collide with limits on resources, creativity and outside providers. In the speaker's project, the original version was roughly four times larger than what was finally released.

The speaker notes that players and partners were understanding about these delays, yet the same tolerance would not be accepted for other products Kaspersky releases, since game development is partly an art. The practical takeaway is to plan scope realistically and expect that the first concept will shrink before release.

talks.title: How you leak your data online
talks.teaser: Explains how fake messages and look-alike pages trick victims into handing over logins and card details, and how to spot them.
talks.summary:
This short awareness video opens with a common scenario: a message that seems to come from a friend, a bank security service, or tech support, linking to a page that asks for account credentials. The speaker explains that a friend's message is often sent by a criminal who has already taken over that friend's account, and that a bank or tech support message can be just as fake. Entering details on the fraudulent page gives the criminal access to the account. This kind of fraud, which tries to extract information that can be turned into money, is called phishing. Common channels include email, social networks, instant messengers and SMS, and fraudsters also use phone calls, such as someone posing as a tax office asking the victim to confirm card details.

The middle of the talk focuses on how to recognise a fake site. Scammers can copy a company's logo and page design, but they usually cannot use the official address, so the domain is often slightly altered. Look-alike spellings, swapped letters or an added word are typical warning signs. Rather than clicking a link in a message, the speaker recommends typing the address manually. A crossed-out padlock or a "not secure" label in the address bar means data sent to that site is not encrypted, so nothing should be entered there.

The closing point is that no legitimate organisation needs passwords, security codes or similar secrets over the phone, whoever the caller claims to be. The practical takeaway is to treat any unsolicited request for secret information as a likely scam, and to verify it through a separate, trusted channel before acting.

talks.title: Home, hybrid or office? How to find the best working format in 2022
talks.teaser: Kaspersky executives and employees share how remote, hybrid and office work affect wellbeing and productivity.
talks.summary:
The pandemic turned a temporary remote-work experiment into a lasting shift, and companies are now rethinking their office plans. Kaspersky's survey on employee wellbeing in the second year of the pandemic found an almost even split: some staff preferred remote work, while others reported exhaustion and isolation. The talk asks how organisations can choose a format that meets staff needs while keeping productivity high.

Speakers described the trade-offs they have seen. One manager found the main downside of remote work to be social, since collaboration and relationship building suffer across time zones. A shift-based team already relied on written communication, documenting everything for postmortems. Kaspersky's communications division moved to hybrid, with two or three office days a week, first-come hot desks and lockers for storing belongings. Staff who chose the office valued in-person interaction, while international teams mostly stayed remote.

Their advice centres on maturity and people. Remote work tests whether processes are documented and repeatable, and public playbooks from fully remote companies such as GitLab are a useful reference. One leader described treating the team like family: holding firm on results while allowing flexible hours when staff face family or health needs, with regular online check-ins that leave room for personal matters. Monthly informal virtual get-togethers were also suggested. The takeaway is to match the format to the team and build connections deliberately.

talks.title: What is Malware?
talks.teaser: Explains what malware is, how it reaches a computer, how to remove it, and how to prevent reinfection.
talks.summary:
This short consumer video explains what malware is and how it reaches a computer. It lists signs that a device may be infected, such as slowdowns, overheating, unfamiliar apps, and crashes. It then describes three infection routes: removable drives borrowed from other people, downloads from pirated or suspicious sources, and malicious links or attachments in spam email.

The video walks through cleanup steps. On a PC, it recommends changing passwords that may have been exposed and updating the software, browser, and operating system. On a Mac, it describes opening Activity Monitor to look for known fake security programs such as Mac Defender, quitting the process, moving the app to the Trash, and emptying the Trash. It then surveys common malware types: keyloggers that record keystrokes, worms that spread across computers and networks, Trojans that delete or alter data, ransomware that locks files for payment, crypto-malware, logic bombs, intrusive adware, spyware, and rootkits and bootkits that give attackers deep access.

To close, the video offers prevention advice. Viewers should download only from trusted sites, check reviews and download counts before installing, question any permissions an app requests, keep software current, and use a VPN on public Wi-Fi. The main takeaway is that most infections come from a small number of everyday habits that users can change.

talks.title: What is Jailbreaking? How to fix a jailbroken iPhone? Is iPhone Jailbreaking Worth the Risks?
talks.teaser: Explains what jailbreaking an iPhone means, the security and warranty risks it carries, and how to restore a jailbroken device.
talks.summary:
Jailbreaking an iPhone removes the restrictions Apple places on its closed iOS, giving the user root access to the operating system. The talk explains that those limits keep apps isolated from one another and ensure that only software Apple has vetted reaches the App Store, which makes it harder for malware to spread. Users often jailbreak to customize their devices or install software from outside the store, although Apple's later fixes have made jailbreaking harder to achieve on many iOS versions.

The risks covered are substantial. A jailbroken phone loses its warranty and automatic updates, and a failed or incompatible update can brick it. Non-approved apps may drain the battery, and access to iCloud, iMessage, FaceTime and Apple Pay can be lost. Crashes, data loss and unreliable calls or location data are more common, and malware from unvetted sources can reach bank details and passwords.

For a device that is already jailbroken, the speaker outlines a recovery path. Back up the phone to iCloud and a computer, turn off Find My, then restore the device through the computer. Choosing the iCloud backup during restore brings the data back, and removing jailbreak apps by hand is unnecessary because the factory reset erases them. If a normal restore fails, recovery mode can erase the device as a last resort. The closing argument is that the added control rarely outweighs the security and usability costs.

talks.title: QR Codes and Security: Stay Safe when QR Code Scanning
talks.teaser: Explains how malicious QR codes lead to phishing, drive-by downloads and device commands, and how to spot them.
talks.summary:
QR codes are now common, but most people cannot tell a fake one from a real one. The video explains that a code cannot itself carry malware or be hacked. The danger lies in the destination it opens. Attackers can send scanners to phishing pages that imitate social media or bank login screens, or to pages that start a download as soon as they are visited.

Codes can also carry commands that act on the phone. The video gives examples of a code that saves a fake bank contact so a later scam call seems credible, and codes that place calls, send texts, draft emails with the recipient and subject already filled in, create a social media account, add a calendar event, or join a preferred Wi-Fi network automatically. Another example is a code that quietly tracks location at places such as airports or shopping malls.

The advice is mostly to pause before scanning. Scan only codes from trusted sources, and be suspicious of stickers pasted over posters, codes placed beside trusted brand logos, and shortened links. Check the URL shown after scanning, and find apps through a search engine or the official store rather than a code. Set alerts on bank and card accounts. The video also recommends a QR scanner that checks codes for malicious content and keeps a history of past scans, and warns against posting documents containing QR codes online, since they may hold e-ticket numbers.

talks.title: 11 Internet Safety Tips for Your Online Security
talks.teaser: Offers eleven everyday internet safety tips covering privacy, passwords, public Wi-Fi, suspicious links and data backups.
talks.summary:
The clip frames internet safety as protecting both your wallet and your reputation. On privacy, it advises against giving strangers online details such as your home address, phone number or relationship status, and recommends switching on privacy settings on social media, since hackers and marketers draw on posts and browsing habits. Closing unused shopping, social and email accounts is presented as a way to reduce the chances of a break-in.

The middle section covers risky browsing and downloads. Shocking ads or links should be skipped, and any link requesting personal data should be avoided even when it appears to come from a bank, because it may be a trap or carry malware. Apps should be checked before installation, with suspicious ones or those from untrusted sites left alone. On networks, sensitive information should stay off unsecured connections, and a VPN is recommended on public Wi-Fi. For accounts, the clip suggests passwords of at least 16 characters mixing numbers and special characters, kept in a password manager, and shopping only on sites whose address begins with https.

The final part addresses lasting exposure and recovery. Posts and photos can persist as copies even after deletion, so anything you would not want an employer or family to see should stay offline. Fake social profiles are flagged as a common route to personal data, so new contacts deserve skepticism. Keeping antivirus updated and backing up data regularly are presented as protection against scams and ransomware.

talks.title: how to recover your app
talks.teaser: Shows how to regain access to accounts after losing the phone that runs your authenticator app.
talks.summary:
Losing a phone that holds an authenticator app can lock you out of accounts protected by one-time codes. The video explains that the first step is to check whether you are still signed in on another device, since many services let you reset the authenticator from the security settings there, or show a secret key or QR code you can re-enter on a new phone. It also warns that this route can fail because web and mobile versions sometimes offer different settings.

When no device is still signed in, the presenter describes alternatives. For large public services such as Google or Facebook, you can start the login with your password and pick a "try another way" option to receive a code by email or text message. For corporate or smaller services, the advice is to contact an administrator or support team and prove account ownership. Once you regain access, link the authenticator to your new phone.

The second half focuses on preventing a repeat of the problem. Store the 16-character secret key or the setup QR code somewhere safe, such as a password manager's secure notes, or save the QR image there. Cloud-syncing the authenticator is another option, and Microsoft Authenticator can use a Microsoft account, though it has backup compatibility issues across operating systems. Google Authenticator can export existing tokens as one large QR code, which you can screenshot and store securely.

talks.title: The Lifecycle of Ransomware Gangs
talks.teaser: Explains why ransomware gangs often vanish soon after rising to prominence, and whether they truly return.
talks.summary:
Ransomware gangs increasingly target large organizations, yet many disappear soon after drawing public attention. This interview explores why and whether these groups are really gone. The researchers say the average lifespan of a gang, once around one and a half to two years, is now shorter. Groups often rebrand or form new gangs when pressure rises. Avaddon, for example, shut down in June and gave decryption keys to nearly 3,000 victims.

Pressure from law enforcement, the threat of arrest and public attention are the main reasons groups disband. DarkSide lost its servers, blog and payment system after the Colonial Pipeline attack, and a group called BlackMatter appeared months later, which the researchers believe is a rebrand. A typical cycle starts with a ransomware-as-a-service model, where affiliates infect networks. A high-profile hit draws more affiliates, then a bigger target and a misstep bring attention that often ends the group, usually within about a year. Babuk instead stopped attacking after a police data leak, rented its leak site to other groups, and later had its source code published.

Larger, well-funded groups can last longer. One was linked to about 400 attacks in two years, and another made eight major changes to its ransomware over that period. One prolific group drew comments from senior politicians, went offline, returned, and was finally taken down through international cooperation. The researchers say operators now mostly communicate privately, and they expect new groups to keep appearing. Because ransomware can harm employees and customers, sometimes with real-world consequences, they stress that awareness and cooperation remain important.

talks.title: What Advanced Threat Actors Got Up to in Q3 2021
talks.teaser: Quarterly review of advanced threat actor activity in Q3, covering DNS hijacking, commercial spyware boot kits and defensive advice.
talks.summary:
Ariel Jungheit and David M of Kaspersky's research team review how the advanced persistent threat landscape changed in the third quarter. The standout case was the SolarWinds-linked activity of Dark Halo, which stayed inside networks for months. Later, a DNS hijacking campaign redirected government mail traffic to fake webmail pages and delivered a backdoor called Tomiris. Tomiris resembles a second-stage tool tied to Dark Halo and shares some overlaps with a backdoor linked to another group, but not enough for a firm link, so shared authorship or development practices remain possible.

The interview also covers FinSpy, a commercial surveillance tool. Kaspersky's four-part private report covered its Windows, Linux and macOS versions. Investigations traced installers backdoored with Metasploit stagers, which led to a FinSpy for PC deployment with UEFI boot kit capability. Separately, a Middle East campaign against government and telecom organisations used a kernel-module framework with UEFI and MBR boot kits, plus Throwback and Slingshot from a commercial penetration testing toolkit.

On regional activity, the guests warn that quarter-to-quarter peaks and dips may be temporary or reflect limited visibility, so long-term conclusions are unwise. Methods include DNS hijacking, a tampered fingerprint scanner package on a distribution server and low-level boot kits, though social engineering remains widespread. Their advice centres on current threat intelligence, endpoint detection and response, network detection of targeted attacks and staff awareness training against phishing.

talks.title: how to protect your profile?
talks.teaser: Explains how Instagram ban attacks work and which steps can help keep an account from being blocked.
talks.summary:
The video describes "ban attacks" against Instagram accounts, in which an attacker gets a profile blocked even though the owner has posted nothing questionable. It outlines two methods. The first floods Instagram's support team with complaints about suicide-related content, often sent with open-source scripts, so that accounts get blocked without careful review. The second files impersonation complaints against the victim, using a stolen verified account that copies the victim's page, avatar and description. Victims can only appeal through the app, and the speaker warns against paying anyone promising to restore an account, since those offers may come from the attackers themselves.

The main protective measure is getting a verified badge, which requires coverage in several independent news sources and a documented application. Users who cannot get verified can make the account private, so only approved followers see posts, and should keep the follower list free of suspicious or empty accounts. Businesses that must stay public are advised to avoid a real face as the avatar, because impersonation complaints work best against profiles that show the owner's photo. A logo or other representative image is suggested instead.

Finally, the speaker recommends keeping a current email address and phone number on the profile so that ownership can be proven during an appeal. Saving content with Instagram's profile backup feature makes it easier to move material to another account if the original is lost.

talks.title: How to run alliances and cooperate with nonprofit organizations
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for How to run alliances and cooperate with nonprofit organizations.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Christina Shingareva, Head of External Relations at Kaspersky, discusses how businesses can build effective alliances and cooperate with nonprofit organizations to tackle cybersecurity threats at scale. She explains that while cybersecurity threats have become mainstream public knowledge, the amplified visibility stems from organizations uniting to research and solve issues collaboratively.

## Key Topics

### No More Ransom Project
Launched in 2016 by Europol, the Netherlands Police, Kaspersky, and McAfee, this initiative helps ransomware victims recover encrypted data for free without paying criminals. Kaspersky experts locate decryption keys for various ransomware families and share them. The project now has over 160 global partners and represents a collaborative approach to a problem without a universal single-day solution.

### Coalition Against Stalkerware
Created at the end of 2019, this coalition addresses "surveillance phone" applications sold legally as parental controls but used for tracking and abuse. Currently includes over 40 partner organizations—cybersecurity companies, academia, domestic violence service organizations, law enforcement, and Interpol as a supporter. The coalition recognized stalkerware as both a technical and social issue requiring diverse expertise.

### Tinycheck Tool
An open-source, free scanning tool developed by Kaspersky in response to a French NGO's request. It runs on Raspberry Pi or Linux devices to detect stalkerware by scanning outgoing traffic without alerting the abuser—critical since stalkerware can notify abusers of detection attempts, potentially escalating domestic violence. The tool is designed for use only by NGOs with trained representatives alongside victims to develop safety and escape plans.

## Technical Details
Stalkerware detection presents a regulatory challenge: Kaspersky can detect stalkerware but cannot flag it as malicious or block it due to its legal status. The response was deploying privacy alerts in products that explicitly explain surveillance capabilities (location tracking, text/call interception, activity monitoring) to users.

## Takeaways
- Successful coalitions address real external needs rather than artificial problems
- Partnerships work best when partners possess fundamentally different expertise
- Social issue projects require significant time and resources; the No More Ransom project continues after five years; Coalition Against Stalkerware remains in early stages after two years
- Direct business profit is unlikely; internal organizational buy-in requires substantial PR and reputation investment to justify initiatives without immediate financial returns

talks.title: How to speak with the C-level about cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Explains how security specialists can frame risk in executive terms and build trust with C-level leaders.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses a familiar gap between security teams and business leaders. The speaker, a chief executive from the Kaspersky group, argues that people who brief chairmen and general directors need to speak the same language as the business. Executives care less about malware counts or attack techniques than about risk, profit, market position, events and competitors, so a security message has to be framed around those concerns.

His main advice is to invest much more time in preparation, starting with an understanding of the executive's agenda. Relationships come before pitches: the presenter should listen to the customer first, avoid focusing on their own products, and work to establish a matching level of confidence on both sides.

He also points to crises, such as a damaged customer relationship or a significant project that has gone wrong, as a rare chance to stand out. When nobody else wants to step forward, taking leadership lets a security professional deliver an unwelcome but honest message and build a new kind of working relationship with senior leaders.
