talks.title: 6 Years of Covert Surveillance in the Middle East
talks.teaser: Follows a six-year espionage campaign against Persian speakers in Iran and how its malware hid inside Chrome and Telegram shortcuts.
talks.summary:
Ferocious Kitten is an advanced threat group that has been running covert surveillance against Persian-speaking people in Iran since at least 2015. The campaign came to light when a researcher posted a tweet about an unknown malware sample along with a screenshot of its lure document, which had been uploaded to VirusTotal. The team decided to trace who was behind the document template and the story of the campaign, because the malware had already been flagged by several security products but nobody had studied it in depth.

The malware was a custom tool used for about six years and gradually improved with bug fixes and new features. It was not especially sophisticated, but it did its job: it took screenshots, logged keystrokes, and searched for Office documents, KeePass password databases, GPG keys, and chat or email records. For persistence, it avoided registry run keys and instead hijacked the shortcuts for Chrome and Telegram. When a user launched either application, the malware ran first and then opened the real program.

The researchers found overlaps with other regional groups such as Charming Kitten and Domestic Kitten, including interest in KeePass and fake VPN client applications. They could not confirm a direct link, since these tools are widely used in the country and make natural targets for many actors. The main takeaway is that detecting a sample is different from understanding the campaign behind it, and that shared regional targets and techniques can blur attribution.

talks.title: How to protect your home Wi-Fi from neighbors
talks.teaser: Shows homeowners how to spot unwanted devices on their Wi-Fi and harden the router with a few practical settings.
talks.summary:
The video explains how to tell whether someone else is using a home Wi-Fi network. Slowdowns in video or games can signal extra connections, and the router's list of connected devices is the place to check. Any device the viewer does not recognize should be removed. If the router's settings are hard to navigate, the video suggests using a visual network map from a security product instead.

The main part covers four hardening steps. First, use a strong network password, since short, common or written-down passwords invite intruders, and expect to reconnect appliances afterwards. Second, change the router's administrator login, because factory credentials are widely published and can let attackers turn a device into part of a DDoS attack. Third, turn off WPS, whose eight-digit PIN can be brute-forced within hours and lets anyone in range connect. Fourth, enable WPA2 encryption, with WPA3 offering stronger protection where the router supports it.

The talk then covers guest networks, which provide internet access without default reach into other local devices, and recommends giving them a separate password. It also notes that stuttering may come from physical obstacles or too many devices competing for bandwidth rather than from intruders. Finally, it advises using a VPN on public Wi-Fi, such as in a coffee shop, to keep data private.

talks.title: A mutual choice: how employers match with their candidates
talks.teaser: Covers how employers build appeal for top talent, what recruiters look for in candidates, and how hiring adapted during the pandemic.
talks.summary:
A senior recruitment manager for Europe explains how employers attract top talent in a market where regional mindsets shape what candidates value. Europe, she notes, puts strong weight on work-life balance. Her suggestions for employers include sharpening recruitment marketing, training recruiters, writing clear job descriptions, and offering flexible working, meaningful autonomy, and visible paths to growth so staff feel their work matters.

Turning to the pandemic, she describes how lockdowns pushed hiring fully online and forced companies to adapt their selection and onboarding, while the information security sector stayed comparatively buoyant and drew in people released by restructuring elsewhere. She expects remote recruiting and a more global job market to stick. On what she looks for, she lists a mix of hard and soft skills, stable work history, reputation, a commitment to ongoing learning, curiosity, preparation for interviews, and communication skills. She says her team does not screen candidates' personal social media, citing legal limits and personal privacy, though it does consider professional profiles.

For young people starting out, her advice centres on a clear plan, continuous education, persistence, and grabbing internships and relevant experience. She warns that entry-level roles often involve routine operational work, which is the necessary path to growth.

talks.title: Protecting against unknown threats: using honeypots
talks.teaser: Shows how a basic SSH honeypot is deployed to capture brute-force login attempts and turn them into defensive data.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces honeypots as decoy systems that imitate vulnerable internet-facing devices, such as cameras, light bulbs and home appliances. Instead of exposing real equipment, a defender places these decoys on the public internet to attract scans, exploits and new attack techniques. Because no legitimate user should ever reach a decoy, any connection to one is a meaningful signal. The speaker presents honeypots as an extra layer that complements endpoint protection and managed detection services rather than replacing them.

The discussion then covers a partnership model in which a provider runs the honeypot infrastructure while the customer deploys sensor nodes in its own network. Collected connections are aggregated and analysed, and partners receive statistics, reused attacker passwords and other artifacts useful for research. The demonstration sets up a basic SSH honeypot in a Docker container, forwarding incoming traffic from port 22 to a listener on port 2222. Within moments the decoy records login attempts using common username and password pairs such as root and admin.

For practitioners, the takeaway is that the logs can be parsed to block offending addresses at the edge firewall or to search for specific credentials, and archiving them supports threat research. The speaker advises stopping the honeypot once it is no longer needed. The closing message is that honeypots catch many threats but not all, so they should be combined with a complete security solution.

talks.title: “To boldly go”: what makes an APT research successful
talks.teaser: Kaspersky's GReAT director recounts how his team hunts novel attacks, names threats, and advises newcomers to the field.
talks.summary:
Costin Raiu, director of Kaspersky's Global Research and Analysis Team, begins with how he entered security: as a high school student in the early 1990s he wrote a custom antivirus script for a virus that commercial products could not clean. He then explains what makes research worth pursuing, namely attacks that are new, rarely seen, and able to affect many users, such as supply chain compromises or low-level persistence that swaps out core system routines. He recalls a Windows kernel privilege escalation zero day he reported to Microsoft in the 1990s, which took months of emails before the company acknowledged and patched it, and a promised souvenir that never arrived.

The talk then turns to naming. The researcher who discovers a threat chooses its name, avoiding copyrighted terms and the names suggested by malware authors, and often drawing on science fiction. He describes the April 2016 discovery of Duqu 2, which began with a late-night message and a sample of several hundred kilobytes. The team linked it to Duqu 1, believed three zero days were used, reported the flaws to Microsoft, and published a technical report.

He closes by arguing that threat volume is outpacing the number of experts, so information sharing and trust between researchers matter. For newcomers, he recommends learning C or C++, then reverse engineering and YARA-based threat hunting.

talks.title: How to create a winning marketing campaign
talks.teaser: Explains how Kaspersky's B2B marketing team plans, runs and measures product campaigns, with revenue as the key success metric.
talks.summary:
Alexander Paotoa, head of the B2B product marketing campaigns team at Kaspersky, opens by describing his remit. His team runs product-focused campaigns for small, medium and enterprise business segments, and he also oversees marketing communication across the distribution chain, including resellers and distributors. He frames marketing as understanding customers and keeping close relationships with them.

He explains that customers do not need to know the technology behind a product. Messages should sound like a relaxed business conversation with a clear commercial purpose. His team equips sales managers with materials so they can deliver simple, clear messages to prospects. He describes the campaign lifecycle as planning, creation, development, enabling and then analysis, which involves many departments across roughly half the company. Close collaboration between those groups keeps delays low and quality high, even though many things can go wrong.

On measurement, he sets aside a long list of tracking platforms. He names Adobe Analytics, Salesforce and Marketo among the tools the company uses, along with other performance marketing systems. His main takeaway is that revenue is the clearest evidence that a marketing campaign has worked.

talks.title: How to configure Telegram to make it truly secure
talks.teaser: Shows how to lock down Telegram with secret chats, passcode protection, two-step verification and tighter privacy settings.
talks.summary:
The talk explains that Telegram's default cloud chats use transport encryption, which hides traffic from outside parties such as an internet provider but leaves message content readable by Telegram itself. Secret chats, by contrast, use end-to-end encryption and keep messages only on the participants' devices. They cannot be created as group chats or used in the web and Windows versions, and they are bound to the device where they began, so a lost or replaced phone means starting over. A padlock icon beside a contact's name marks a secret chat.

To protect the app and the account, the presenter recommends enabling a passcode lock with a short auto-lock interval, plus fingerprint unlock where the device supports it. Two-step verification adds an extra account password that is required at each new login. The speaker warns that forgetting this password forces an account reset with a seven-day wait, after which the account and its chats are erased, so the password should be stored in a password manager.

The privacy menu can hide the phone number from strangers, restrict last-seen and online status to nobody, and limit calls, group invitations and profile photos to contacts. For stronger anonymity, the talk suggests a non-temporary separate phone number, secret chats with a secure connection to conceal the IP address, self-destructing timers, and screenshot alerts that do not work on macOS. It closes by noting that Signal or Threema may suit users who need the highest level of secrecy.

talks.title: Pain in The Neck | 15-minute Yoga for tech neck
talks.teaser: A guided yoga sequence eases neck stiffness and posture strain for people who spend long hours at their devices.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this session presented in partnership with Kaspersky, yoga teacher and personal trainer Shona Vertue leads a 15-minute physical routine tailored specifically for individuals suffering from "tech neck"—strain caused by hovering over digital devices throughout the day. Framing the session around the idea that updating software or phones can feel like a nuisance, Vertue notes that physical posture also requires regular resets and patches to keep moving smoothly and prevent physical decline.

### Key Topics
- Counteracting Tech Neck: Addressing the physical strain, neck stiffness, and poor spinal alignment resulting from long hours spent bent over screens and handheld devices.
- Controlled Articular Rotations (CARs): Isolating joint movements to evaluate, maintain, and expand true active mobility without compensatory shifting from the torso or hips.
- Postural Strength and Spinal Health: Moving through spinal extension, flexion, and lateral stretches to relieve compression and reset posture.
- Glute and Core Activation: Engaging stabilizing muscles such as the glutes and core to protect the lower back and support optimal movement patterns.

### Technical Details
- Neck Controlled Articular Rotations & Range Checks: Participants brace the spine, arm, and chest muscles by making fists, then guide the chin down, laterally toward the collarbone, and into slow, controlled circles. This isolates neck mobility from chest or hip compensation. This is followed by head turns to observe lateral discrepancies, reinforcing that mobility operates on a "use it or lose it" principle.
- Forearm, Chest, and Lateral Stretches: Interlaced finger extensions over the head stretch the forearms and fingers. Combining hand-behind-head thoracic extension with forward flexion synchronizes movement with breathing, followed by seated side bends keeping the opposite hip anchored to elongate the spine.
- Cat-Cow and Contralateral Stability: On all fours, participants mobilize the spine vertebra by vertebra. Contralateral extensions (bird-dog variations) require extending one leg back while keeping a neutral lumbar spine (avoiding an arched "banana back") via core bracing and glute contraction, pairing arm extensions and bringing knee to elbow.
- Pigeon Pose Variation: Transitioning from all fours by extending one leg back and externally rotating the front leg, participants sink hips back toward the floor. To build active hip and leg strength rather than purely passive stretching, participants perform pulses where fingertips lift off the floor.
- Active Cobra and Floor Cooldown: Lying prone, active cobra repetitions emphasize chin retraction, shoulder blade retraction, glute contraction, and engagement of back extensors. The routine concludes with wide-knee child's pose, supine knee-to-chest rocking, Pavanamuktasana (wind-removing pose) to massage the ascending colon, gentle spinal twists, and a brief resting breathwork sequence.

### Takeaways
- Routine physical breaks are vital to protect posture and mobility when working long hours around digital technology.
- True mobility requires isolated joint control; compensating with other body parts masks mobility deficits.
- Combining active glute engagement and core stability safeguards the lumbar spine during movement.
- Taking a short break for physical recovery pairs naturally with taking time to let devices run necessary resets and updates.

talks.title: Eugene Kaspersky’s Proven Way to Stop Smoking
talks.teaser: A former long-time smoker describes the mental method that helped him quit for good.
talks.summary:
This talk is a personal account of quitting smoking rather than a technical security topic. The speaker, a long-time heavy smoker, explains why earlier attempts failed, including a self-help book that focused on money saved. Instead, he asked what smoking actually gave him, concluded that it gave him nothing, and listed what bothered him most: the harm to his health, the constant smell of tobacco, and the way he felt before important negotiations.

He then describes the method he used. First, identify what you dislike most about smoking. Second, build that dislike into a strong mental trigger, which he calls a big red button in the brain. Third, choose a specific day, in his case his birthday, as the last day you smoke. On that day, smoke the final cigarette, reflect on your dislike, and press the button before going to bed. He says he woke up a non-smoker the next morning and now feels happy when he sees someone smoking.

He also admits that he had quit once before and relapsed. He told himself that an occasional cigarette was harmless, and his use gradually grew from once a month to once a week and then to several times a day until he started again. His closing advice is that quitting must allow no exceptions, not even occasional cigars or cigarettes, and should be done firmly and permanently.

The lesson starts from the point that a large amount of information about most people already exists online, from anything posted or sent online to confidential data shared with banks. Massive data leaks have reached record levels in recent years, so more personal data is circulating and more of it is vulnerable. Anyone who wants to harm or profit from a person can go after that data, whether for extortion, financial scams or impersonation. Even careful people who limit how and with whom they share information are not fully protected, since abusers may turn to the black market for details such as login information for social media accounts.

The talk then shows how stolen data is traded on dark net forums and markets, where it is cheap. Prices quoted include ID card data at five cents to ten dollars, passport scans at six to fifteen dollars, medical records at one to thirty dollars, credit card details at six to twenty dollars, and online banking and PayPal accounts at fifty to five hundred dollars. Buyers use this data for extortion, spam and phishing, direct theft, and reputational or social damage. The lesson also gives a fictional case: a man named Jack had a selfie with his passport used to make fraudulent sales. Deceived buyers went to the police with the photo, and Jack was detained until the matter was cleared up. He lost time and peace of mind and never learned how the photo had leaked.

The closing point is that people cannot be sure all their data is safe. The lesson says the next lesson will cover the specific ways a person can be doxxed, so that viewers can recognize them.

It urges teachers in particular to watch what they post, repost and like on social media, since students may notice those interactions, and it notes that content involving profanity, alcohol or adult material deserves extra care.

The second part covers work email. An account used for professional purposes represents the employer, so writers should give each message a specific subject line that makes it easy to find later, use reply all when several people are copied, and finish with a signature showing their position, company and website. Work addresses should not be used for personal sign-ups or shopping, users should log out when checking mail on a shared computer, and replies should not be delayed.

The final section addresses behavior on social networks. Users should remember that a real person is on the other end of every exchange, avoid hurtful or bullying language, and show the same respect online as they would offline. For anyone facing cyberbullying, the advice is to avoid answering the aggressors, to block them with the platform's built-in feature, and to contact site administrators, who can remove posts and stop further messages. The video closes by noting that bullying has real consequences, including withdrawal from social activity, depression, sleep problems and weaker schoolwork, so it should be addressed quickly.

The first suggested topic is an introductory class on how the internet works, its history and how it may develop, along with the devices that connect to it and the services students use for watching content, communicating and research. The second covers common scams, especially phishing and fraud carried out through phone calls or messaging apps, and the channels scammers use to spread their messages. The third addresses cyberbullying, covering its types and how to avoid becoming a target. The fourth focuses on finding information and uses fake news as an example. Students should check a source, read beyond a clickbait headline, compare other posts by the same author, and confirm whether a story is a repost of older news.

The talk closes by pointing to supporting material, including Kaspersky blog articles, quarterly and yearly threat reports, and a children's book about cyberbullying that can serve as a teaching resource. talks.title: Cybershare: Threat Intelligence
talks.teaser: Recounts the 2017 Ex-Petya outbreak and argues why threat intelligence matters for organisations, especially in the UK.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by asking whether threat intelligence and attribution are worth the effort, and whether knowing who is attacking you changes anything. It then looks back at the Ex-Petya outbreak of 2017. The malware spread from Ukraine through a compromised finance and accounting package that companies there were required to use. It reused the same vulnerabilities that WannaCry had already exploited to get onto victims' machines.

Ex-Petya initially resembled a Petya ransomware family, showing the same ransom message and similar early behaviour. It turned out to have no way to reverse its encryption, so it acted as a wiper that destroyed data. Shipping group Maersk and pharmaceutical firm Merck were hit as collateral damage, and the speaker notes that Maersk's environment went down within 15 minutes. Maersk recovered largely because two backup servers in Africa had been offline and were not infected. Staff flew out with USB sticks to bring the data back, and about 40,000 workstations were restored within ten days.

The speaker argues that the lesson has not fully taken hold. Large organisations with big security budgets and SOC teams still fall to ransomware families that exploit known vulnerabilities, as several recent high-profile victims show. Progress toward intelligence-led defence is slow, with the UK still early in adoption for most organisations while some other regions are further along. The takeaway for practitioners is that understanding the threats aimed at their own technology estate remains a priority.

talks.title: Cybershare: Threat Intelligence
talks.teaser: Discusses whether threat intelligence and attribution matter to businesses and how tracking adversaries differs from attribution.
talks.summary:
The discussion opens by asking whether threat intelligence and attribution are worth the effort for an organization, and whether knowing who is attacking changes anything. The speakers separate commodity threats, such as common malware and cybercrime, from bespoke threats aimed at a particular sector or company. They note that both need sound controls and basic cyber hygiene first. They also describe the threat landscape as varying by industry: an oil and gas company, a critical infrastructure operator and a small retailer face different attackers and different budgets.

Threat hunting is presented as the proactive side of intelligence. Teams search their own logs and telemetry for indicators or techniques from feeds, and check whether an activity seen in one department has spread elsewhere. Tracking adversary groups and mapping them to their tools and techniques is described as useful for validating controls. For example, red teams can mimic specific actor types, and the SOC can confirm that its detection rules work. The speakers stress that this kind of tracking is not attribution. In their view, attribution needs prosecution and evidence from government agencies, which a commercial company cannot gather alone.

The takeaway is that the larger gain for the industry lies in helping internal teams do bespoke analysis more efficiently, adding context to threat intelligence, and integrating it through APIs into risk, asset and vulnerability management dashboards. Organizations get the most value when cybersecurity data is used across the whole business rather than in isolation.

talks.title: Threat Intelligence – Part 4 The Way Forward
talks.teaser: Examines whether attribution matters to organisations and how threat intelligence should be scoped to their own risk context.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This discussion explores the practical application and necessity of threat intelligence and cyber attribution for organizations navigating today's threat landscape. The speakers examine whether pinpointing specific adversaries matters to enterprise defense, how organizations can contextualize threat intelligence to fit their business requirements, and how the economic and technological landscape of security operations is shifting.

### Key Topics
- **The Value of Attribution**: The speakers debate whether attributing an attack to a nation-state, cyber criminal gang, or hacktivist makes an operational difference. Attribution is predominantly critical when there are legal or law enforcement implications that require presenting evidence in a court of law. For general defense, attributing mass-scale, sprayed attacks (such as mass scanning or credential brute forcing) is largely impractical, whereas understanding exposure to specific attack patterns—such as MageCart-style tactics—offers direct defensive value.
- **Contextualization and Asset Mapping**: Threat intelligence is defined as a combination of technology and people that must be shaped around an organization's specific threat landscape. Merely ingesting data feeds without correlating them to an internal asset database leads to spiraling costs without actionable cyber risk reduction.
- **Sourcing Diverse Intelligence**: Organizations are advised not to rely on a single vendor or supplier. A resilient threat intelligence capability incorporates open-source intelligence, US-based vendors, Chinese vendors, and built-in intelligence from next-generation SIEM engines and SOC platforms to gain a truly global perspective.
- **Economics and Operational Shifts**: The cost of monitoring and Security Operations Center (SOC) capabilities is decreasing significantly due to automation and modern toolsets. Capabilities that previously cost £50 to £60 per user per month in large multinationals can now be acquired for around £10 per user per month.

### Technical Details
- **Attacks & Threat Vectors**: Covers broad, automated campaigns including mass port/vulnerability scanning, mass credential brute forcing, and web skimming/targeting exemplified by MageCart actors.
- **Infrastructure & Monitoring**: Ingestion of data feeds into next-generation SIEM platforms and SOC architectures, tied directly to an organization's internal asset inventory to prevent data overload and uncontrolled expense.

### Takeaways
- Focus threat intelligence on protecting critical internal assets and understanding relevant adversary TTPs (like MageCart) rather than obsessing over naming individual threat actors, unless preparing cases for law enforcement.
- Contextualize feeds against your business environment and asset databases to control costs and deliver measurable risk reduction.
- Take advantage of descending SOC and monitoring costs brought by next-generation automated tooling, and engage in open public discussions to train the next generation of security professionals.

talks.summary:
### Overview
This walkthrough demonstrates how to set up and configure a corporate workspace within the Kaspersky Security Center Cloud Console to prepare for deploying security solutions across company devices. The process assumes the administrator already holds a single account for Kaspersky products.

### Key Topics
- Connecting to the Kaspersky Security Center Cloud Console and accepting necessary legal agreements.
- Configuring company details, workspace parameters, and selecting appropriate data centers.
- Choosing between commercial activation codes and 30-day trial workspaces.
- Completing the initial setup using the automated Quick Start Wizard.
- Configuring network settings, Kaspersky Security Network (KSN) participation, and deploying Network Agent packages.

### Technical Details
- **Workspace Creation**: Administrators access the cloud console via a web browser under an existing Kaspersky account, accept the agreements and privacy policy, and enter the company and workspace names. The country selected directly determines the data center where operational data is processed (with mappings documented in the online help). Workspace sizing accommodates device counts ranging from 300 to 10,000.
- **Licensing Considerations**: Users can supply a commercial activation code or request a trial workspace. A trial workspace lasts for 30 days only, has specific documented limitations, and the current version does not support migrating settings from a trial workspace to a commercial one.
- **Provisioning Wait Time**: Creation takes time; users must wait for a confirmation email containing the access link rather than clicking immediately on the webpage.
- **Quick Start Wizard**: Launches automatically upon first connection to create necessary policies, tasks, and software installation packages.
- **Agent & Solution Selection**: Requires deploying Kaspersky Network Agent and security applications on target computers. Kaspersky Network Agent for Windows and Kaspersky Endpoint Security for Windows are selected by default. Proxy server parameters can be supplied if endpoints route traffic through a proxy.
- **Kaspersky Security Network (KSN)**: Provides real-time threat intelligence to increase detection rates for emerging threats. Disabling KSN is noted to significantly weaken endpoint protection.
- **Standalone Installation Package**: The wizard generates a unique standalone installation package for the Network Agent. This package is an executable file digitally signed with a Kaspersky certificate, containing the distribution files preconfigured with specific connection parameters for that distinct workspace.

### Takeaways
- Proper initial planning regarding company location is vital because it locks in data center placement.
- Because trial workspace settings cannot be migrated to commercial workspaces in this version, organizations should evaluate whether a trial or immediate commercial deployment is appropriate.
- The Quick Start Wizard automates the core baseline—generating workspace-specific, signed Network Agent packages, default tasks, and policies—to streamline endpoint onboarding.

talks.title: How to optimize Windows 10 for gaming & performance in 2020
talks.teaser: Explains practical Windows 10 tweaks like network checks, power settings and antivirus gaming modes to reduce in-game lag.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the frustration of lag or freezes during online matches and argues that most of these stalls come from software-side causes that can be fixed. It walks through seven tips aimed at modern gamers.

On the network side, it recommends checking speed and ping with an online test, noting that a typical fiber connection is fine for most games while delays in the hundreds of milliseconds are a real obstacle. Remedies include repositioning the router, switching to a wired link, or changing provider. For graphics, it advises lowering detail or resolution until frame rates hold steady, with more than 60 FPS preferred for online play. Laptops should run on AC power in the best performance mode. Task Manager can be used to sort processes by memory and CPU to spot resource-hungry apps such as forgotten messengers. The antivirus section argues that disabling or removing security software is counterproductive, since Windows Defender may step in and some products offer a gaming mode that suppresses pop-ups and scans. Scheduled scans and Windows Update should be set outside gaming hours, and periodic cleanup of temporary files and unused games keeps the system responsive.

The closing message is that a clean, well-configured system with a suitable security product in gaming mode should remove most performance-related losses, leaving the outcome to tactics and teamwork.

talks.title: What is cloud computing and how can it benefit your business?
talks.teaser: Explains the main cloud computing models and how security as a service fits into a business's choices.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by describing cloud computing as access to computing resources and programs delivered over the internet, and stresses that the right option depends on what a business needs. It covers infrastructure as a service, which supplies virtual processing power, storage or networking, and how those resources can be delivered through public, private or hybrid models. Public clouds offer scalability and flexibility with shared capacity run by outside vendors. Private clouds give a single organization dedicated, customizable access over a secure network and more control. Hybrid setups let a company use public capacity when demand rises while keeping sensitive data off third-party systems.

The second part covers software as a service, in which a provider hosts applications on its own infrastructure and makes them available to customers online. Cloud-based cybersecurity is given as an example, sometimes called security as a service. It runs on individual devices without on-premise installation, and the vendor maintains and updates virus and malware profiles, so users stay protected across all their devices.

The closing segment wraps up the explainer and points viewers to a Kaspersky resource for finding the right cloud solution for their business.

talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning A preview of Black Hat 2020 with Kurt Baumgartner.
talks.summary:
## Overview
This Black Hat 2020 preview talk discusses significant cybersecurity campaigns and threat actor activities observed in 2019 and early 2020, focusing on targeted exploitation of activists and evolving Russian threat actor tactics.

## Key Campaigns
The speaker highlights a campaign targeting Hong Kong activists through forum-based water holes in January. A full iOS/iPhone exploit and malware implant chain was discovered and analyzed, revealing the implants were under active development with modifications made over several months.

## Russian Threat Actor Evolution
The speaker references a 2018 security analyst summit presentation on Russian threat actors (referred to as "bears") and their strategic shift eastward. A key prediction—that traditional flagship implants like x-agent (also called splm) would decline—has materialized. By early 2020, new .NET variants of x-tunnel were observed in Central European telecom targets, indicating a broader shift toward zebra-c tooling rather than traditional malware families. Traditional tools like splm downloaders have "completely fallen off the map," replaced by newer, lower-volume downloaders and server-side approaches.

## Server-Side Scanning Tactics
Throughout 2019, multiple reports documented Russian threat actors scanning Exchange servers for vulnerabilities. Interest also extended to SQL servers and SMB servers exposed on the internet, representing a significant tactical shift from traditional malware deployment toward reconnaissance and precise server-side targeting.

## Attribution Challenges
The speaker discusses uncertainty around attribution of activity to "cozy duke," noting a lack of direct evidence linking wellness-related findings to this group. Despite statements attributing this activity to cozy duke, the speaker indicates ongoing investigation and plans for colleagues to present more detailed findings at a future webinar. Activity has been tracked since 2018.

## Takeaways
Russian threat actor behavior continues evolving toward targeted server-side scanning, precision targeting in Asia and Central Asia, and away from traditional implant deployment. Attribution remains complex, with public statements sometimes outpacing investigative confidence.

talks.title: Account setup (security fundamentals)
talks.teaser: Covers basic account security for gaming services, including strong passwords, two-factor authentication, and mailbox protection.
talks.summary:
This lesson from a gaming security course introduces the basic account protections that most gaming services share. It starts with passwords, which should be at least ten characters long, mix upper and lower case letters, numbers and special characters, and never be reused across services, so that one hacked account does not expose the others. A password manager is suggested for anyone who finds many unique credentials hard to remember.

The lesson then explains that a strong password does not protect against data leaks or theft from the service itself, which is where two-factor authentication helps. The one-time code may arrive by text message, email or a companion app, so the mailbox tied to the account becomes critical. Because gaming accounts are often linked to a main email, that mailbox needs its own strong, unique password and two-factor authentication, and should not be used for dubious sign-ups. Linking a gaming account to corporate mail is discouraged, since leaving the job could mean losing the account and its games.

The lesson closes with other recommendations: make the profile private so strangers cannot see which games are played or how many hours are spent on them, and after using someone else's device, log out remotely through the account settings. Viewers are asked to check these settings now, with platform-specific steps promised in later lessons.

talks.title: Account hijacking and how to avoid it
talks.teaser: Explains how game accounts get hijacked and which habits, such as avoiding account trading, keep them safe from theft and scams.
talks.summary:
Game accounts are valuable targets because they hold purchased games and in-game items. Criminals usually steal them to resell, and sometimes to send phishing links to other players by exploiting the genuine owner's good reputation. Most thefts are random, so even an account with few games is at risk. Recovering a stolen account through the service's support team is possible in theory, but the process is slow, may fail if staff doubt ownership, and may not return the items, as the Steam terms state.

The talk then turns to prevention. Paying strangers to boost an account often means losing it, and sharing an account with friends exposes it to their weaker security and to later disputes. Buying an account is risky because it may be stolen or tied to fraud, and platform rules forbid transfers, so the buyer never becomes the legal owner. Selling carries its own traps: a buyer may stall until credentials are handed over, or use the account to send phishing messages that are blamed on the seller.

The key takeaways are three rules: never hand over a game account to anyone, even briefly; do not buy accounts; and do not sell them. Following these reduces most of the risk, and account settings that strengthen protection are covered in later lessons.

talks.title: Where to download games safely
talks.teaser: Explains how to get games from official stores while avoiding phishing links, malware downloads and scam key sellers.
talks.summary:
The lesson starts from one principle: a game should come from an official store. It names major PC platforms such as Steam, Epic Games Store and GOG, plus Google Play and the App Store for phones. Big official stores are presented as safer because they guard their reputation and vet what they host, and as more convenient for collecting a whole library in one place.

Fortnite serves as the main example. Epic Games first kept the game off Google Play and steered Android users to its own website. When Google Play lacked it, some people turned to third-party sites and downloaded malware instead. Installing from the website meant allowing unknown sources, and some never switched that setting off again. Epic listed the game on Google Play in spring 2020. Scams also arrive by message: a forum post promising a beta download link likely leads to malware that can enlist a computer in a botnet, send spam or flood it with ads, while an email with a Steam add-on offer likely leads to a fake page that steals login details to hijack the account. Links in emails, messages, social networks, messengers or forums should never be used for downloads.

Digital key marketplaces get a warning as well. Some small stores are legitimate, but they are hard to tell apart from malicious ones, and scammers sometimes use well-known marketplaces too. Victims pay by card and get a useless code or nothing back. The takeaway is to avoid third-party sites, even when the keys look cheap.

He argues that businesses in fast-moving sectors need the same periodic adjustment, and he points to games and cybersecurity as examples.

He then contrasts the two markets through a musical lens. Games, he suggests, resemble heavy rock, with audiences that are intensely engaged. Cybersecurity, by comparison, often plays in the background like quiet lobby music that people barely notice.

His closing point is that cybersecurity matters too much to stay unnoticed, so consumer messaging has to change. It should be less intense than gaming but more dynamic than elevator music. The goal is to help people see how much their increasingly connected lives depend on security.

talks.title: How to integrate Kaspersky Endpoint Security for Linux into Jenkins
talks.teaser: Shows how Kaspersky Endpoint Security for Linux scans Docker images for malicious files inside Jenkins CI/CD pipelines.
talks.summary:
The video presents an integration of Kaspersky Endpoint Security for Linux 11.1 with Jenkins, framed as a way to bring malware scanning into continuous integration and delivery pipelines. Jenkins starts local scan tasks on an agent host where the security product is installed. The demo first points out that, under the endpoint policy, local tasks are off unless users are permitted to view and manage them, so that setting has to change before Jenkins can run anything.

The first scenario is a standalone Jenkins project that starts a container from a parameterised Docker image, records its container ID in a file, and then scans that container. If the scan finds threats, the build is marked as failed. An infected test image produced a failure, while a clean image finished successfully. The second scenario triggers a build from a GitHub webhook whenever a Dockerfile changes. Jenkins pulls the repository, builds the image layer by layer, and sends the result for scanning. A malicious archive was added during the build, so the scan flagged an object in the image, yet the job still reported success because its pass condition was only a correctly formed Dockerfile.

The closing part shows the matching detection events in Kaspersky Security Center. The practical takeaway is that scan results can gate pipeline stages, but the pass condition should be chosen deliberately, since a build can succeed while malicious content is present unless an additional check is added to the script.

talks.title: Team works remotely - how to keep supporting your customers?
talks.teaser: Outlines how a global support team organizes its tiers, cross-team links and remote work habits.
talks.summary:
The speaker leads a global support team that provides technical help and professional services to customers ranging from home users to large enterprises. Requests typically flow through tiers. Automated self-service, such as a knowledge base, chatbot or suggested fixes, catches the most common problems, and whatever remains goes to a human first-line agent. Harder cases move up to second-line specialists who can analyze complex issues.

The talk then covers how support works with other departments. Recurring problems are passed to development teams so that product changes can reduce the number of tickets reaching support, and feedback from sales helps the team understand what customers actually experience. The shift to remote work is a central theme: tools such as VPN and remote desktop were built for the corporate network, and when staff connect from outside, traffic rises on gateways and front-end servers. Teams need to plan for that extra load across VPN, virtual machines, ticketing, knowledge bases, messengers and the hardware employees use at home, such as laptops, phones and headphones.

For managers working remotely, the speaker's advice is to talk with the team more often than before, check in when something seems wrong, and turn on the camera so people can see each other. Meeting minutes and written protocols are also important, because agreements recorded in email are easier to refer back to than verbal conversations, which now happen less often.

talks.title: Branding and leadership in business: lessons taken from gaming
talks.teaser: Draws brand and leadership lessons from gaming communities, from Discord onboarding to raid team roles and strategic thinking.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how brands can build connection by speaking the way their audience actually talks. The speaker, who leads a global brand communication team at Kaspersky, points to gaming communities as a model. Discord is singled out as a messenger built for gamers, with features shaped around the games people play and playful join messages that greet each new member by name. The core point is that strong brands and ambassadors talk with people rather than at a target audience, in a tone that creates emotional ties.

Next, guild names in World of Warcraft are presented as a form of branding. A name signals the atmosphere in advance, whether that is a social group, a hardcore raiding team or a helpful community, much as product names set expectations. From team play the speaker draws management lessons: each member has a defined role, and a leader must weigh the strengths and weaknesses of the whole group, not only individual skill. A consulting competition case is used to illustrate strategic thinking. The strongest solution came from a player who said raid play had trained him to predict the actions of dozens of people under time pressure.

The closing section highlights leadership and patience as takeaways. The speaker compares her own role at Kaspersky to a Shadow Priest, a class that sometimes has to take damage and sometimes has to strike, all in service of building a better future.

talks.title: How to win when you're working from home? Tips from the Kaspersky team
talks.teaser: Offers practical tips for keeping a home office secure, productive and healthy while working remotely.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses the move to working from home and how to set up a workday that stays productive and balanced. The speaker recommends a dedicated workspace, ideally with a desk that adjusts in height, and keeping working hours fixed at around eight to nine hours so the day does not drift into long evenings. Letting colleagues know when you are available, getting ready as if heading to an office, and focusing on one task at a time are presented as ways to separate work from home life.

On the security side, the speaker covers routine habits: installing software updates promptly, changing passwords often, and running an antivirus product. Connecting through the company VPN is advised. The speaker describes keeping three separate networks at home, one for the family, one for guests, and a private one used only for work. Corporate USB drives and other removable media should be encrypted so the data stays protected if a family member borrows the device by mistake. Locking the laptop whenever stepping away and keeping children away from it round out the advice.

Health gets attention as well. Short breaks to stand, walk or take a breath, drinking water through the day, and a physical routine in the morning such as push-ups, sit-ups or a stationary bike ride are suggested. The closing message is that a home office should be a deliberately organised, protected space where good routines and security habits support each other.

talks.title: How to meet customers’ demands and maintain work-life balance
talks.teaser: Shows how security services fit customer demands and how to protect personal time by scheduling personal values.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with how customers buy security help. Small and mid-sized businesses often hand off detection and monitoring to an MSP or MSSP, which avoids investing in on-premise infrastructure and frees their IT staff for business priorities. Larger enterprises with limited skilled staff want more from vendors: on-site tools their own analysts can use, such as searching for indicators of compromise from a discovered campaign or writing rules that catch other variants of the same threat. Many of these organizations also want outside help with threat analysis, threat hunting and training, as a middle path between a full in-house operations center and doing everything alone.

The second half shifts to work-life balance. The speaker's core advice is to identify personal values outside of work, decide which of them are non-negotiable, and then block time for them on the calendar. Sharing a calendar with a partner helps both people keep the same commitments. Emergencies will sometimes override these blocks, but staying consistent with them is the goal.

To stay on top of work, the speaker relies on a disciplined digital calendar with alerts for deadlines and key action items, along with handwritten to-do lists that give a sense of progress as items are checked off. The speaker admits that a mental to-do list can cost sleep but also produces useful ideas. The takeaway is to align the calendar with personal values and then keep that alignment as consistently as possible.

talks.title: Part 7: How to configure password protection
talks.teaser: Shows how to set passwords in a Kaspersky policy so users cannot exit, uninstall or stop endpoint protection.
talks.summary:
The video shows an administrator how to stop users of Kaspersky Endpoint Security and the Kaspersky Network Agent from disabling protection or changing its settings. By default, a local user can exit the protection application from the notification area menu without elevated rights, and the policy does not prevent this. A computer with protection off is more exposed to infection and is marked critical in the administration console, where the monitoring tab lists affected machines. Starting the application again from the console clears the status only briefly, because the user can switch it off again.

The fix is a password set in the policy. Password protection stays active even if the policy is later disabled, so the product cannot be exited without it. The demonstration confirms that the exit option is blocked on the user's computer and that the uninstall button appears dimmed.

The network agent needs separate protection, because a user with administrator rights could remove it and stop the policy from controlling the product. The presenter enables password protection for the agent in the settings section, selects the uninstall password option, makes it required, and saves the policy. After the policy is applied, uninstalling the agent requires a password. The video also notes that the Kaspersky icon can be hidden from the notification area through the interface section of the endpoint policy.

talks.title: Part 6: How to automatically organize computers into groups in Kaspersky Security Center
talks.teaser: Shows how to automatically sort computers into groups in Kaspersky Security Center using relocation rules based on OS and IP.
talks.summary:
Protecting a network with Kaspersky endpoint protection often means servers, desktops and laptops need different settings, yet a single default group applies one policy to every machine. The video explains why grouping helps: each group can carry its own protection parameters, and problem computers are easier to spot. Groups can mirror Active Directory, the corporate structure, user privileges or machine purpose, and folders can be nested without limit.

The demonstration builds a Servers group and a Workstations group with Desktops and Laptops subgroups for a sample company. Automation comes from device relocation rules, each defining what to move, the criteria a machine must satisfy, the destination group and when to apply it. Timing options are a one-time run against existing and newly discovered devices, a run repeated on network agent reinstallation, or a permanent rule that returns manually moved machines to their assigned place. Conditions include a running network agent, operating system version and IP address range. Rules are checked in list order, so the top matching rule is applied.

Rules the console creates automatically, such as when unassigned devices are chosen during remote installation, can be disabled but not edited or deleted. The demo closes by confirming the server sits in the Servers group and the desktop and laptop machines sit in their subgroups. The takeaway is that default settings suit an average user and can be adjusted to balance protection, performance and user experience.

talks.title: Part 5: How to install a Kaspersky Endpoint Security standalone package on a notebook
talks.teaser: Shows how to build and install a Kaspersky Endpoint Security standalone package on a notebook when remote deployment fails.
talks.summary:
This video covers installing Kaspersky Endpoint Security locally on a notebook when remote installation from the administration server fails. It suits environments where only a few computers need manual setup. Running the ordinary installer wizard takes time and invites mistakes, such as mistyping the administration server address, so the recommended approach is a prebuilt package that carries the installation files and settings together.

The administrator creates the package from the installation packages node in Kaspersky Security Center. The wizard can include the network agent, so the target machine connects to the administration server right after installation and can be moved into the managed category. The package can then be saved to a shared folder or flash drive, exported as HTML link code for a web page, or sent by email, where the default mail client opens with the subject and body already filled in and a link to the package.

On the client side, the user downloads the package and runs it, which takes two clicks. If an older version or a third-party protection product is present, a restart may be needed. The computer then connects to the server and is placed in the managed devices group automatically. The video closes with the software version report, which counts Kaspersky application instances across managed computers, including network agents, administration servers and endpoint security instances. The main takeaway is that a prepared standalone package reduces configuration errors on local installs and gives administrators a clear inventory afterward.

talks.title: Part 2: Configure Kaspersky Security Center through the Quick Start Wizard
talks.teaser: Walks through the Kaspersky Security Center Quick Start Wizard, from licensing and proxy setup to updates and remote installation.
talks.summary:
This video shows how to complete the Quick Start Wizard in Kaspersky Security Center the first time an administrator connects to the administration server. Some wizard parameters are filled in automatically, while others must be entered by hand. The wizard offers optional mobile device management, where a license can be added from a key file or through an activation code, or left until later. It then asks for proxy settings so the administration server can reach the internet for updates and Kaspersky Security Network services, and it can check whether newer plugin versions are available and install them.

Next, the administrator accepts the license agreement, reviews the cloud-assisted KSN protection terms, and configures email notifications by entering an address and SMTP server details. Event notifications are not sent by default, so they must be enabled in the event properties. The send test message button sends a check message, but the wizard only reports connection or authentication errors, so the administrator must confirm the message in the inbox. The administration server runs on Windows Server 2016 and uses Microsoft SQL Server 2014 Express to store its data. Installer files can be downloaded from the vendor website or the product page on the support site, and the installation shell lets the user choose components or extract all files to a folder.

Before anything is installed, the wizard checks system requirements, including .NET Framework 4 or later. A leftover network agent or console on a machine without a server blocks the installation, so those must be removed first, while an existing server switches the installer to upgrade mode. The license agreement must be accepted. The standard type installs the server, the console, the web console and a server-version network agent. The custom type lets the user modify the component set, point to a pre-installed external database server and adjust parameters. The chosen network size controls which advanced server functions, such as server hierarchies and access control, are shown, and these settings can be changed later. SQL Server or MySQL can serve as the database, and since version 10 SP3 SQL Server Express must be downloaded manually. Windows authentication is typically used, and local administrator rights are enough when the database sits on the same machine.

Before files are copied, the administrator can go back and revise settings. After installation, selected plugins are added, some of which require accepting extra license terms. The wizard then offers to open the administration console. The initial configuration of the server is left for the next video.

talks.title: Key principles of a successful negotiator: Mowgli and Samurai
talks.teaser: Presents two negotiation principles, one about finding common ground with the other side and one about handling failure and fear.
talks.summary:
The speaker offers two principles for successful negotiation, starting with what they call the Mowgli principle: the people on both sides are fundamentally the same. Buyers and sellers play opposing roles with conflicting goals, one wanting to pay more or less than the other, but a negotiation goes better when it moves from role-to-role interaction to person-to-person, or ideally expert-to-expert, exchange. The speaker warns against being seen as a salesperson pushing a purchase. The advice is to first look for what you have in common with the other person, and to be honest with them.

The second principle, which the speaker calls the samurai principle, is more demanding. Failure is a normal part of life, so a negotiator should be ready to fail from the beginning rather than treat it as a surprise. The speaker stresses suppressing fear, because once fear takes hold, the negotiator loses the moment that matters. The talk ends by noting that these two ideas may sound lighthearted, but the speaker says they have helped in different situations.

This short video introduces Shok-1, an artist who spray paints x-ray style art on walls around the world. He traces the concept to graffiti he first developed in the late 1990s, and he explains that his formal education was in science. For years those two sides of his life stayed separate until they came together in the x-ray style. He says he has always wanted to see what is inside things and how they work, and he frames his murals as a kind of diagnosis. He asks viewers to read the subject the way a doctor reads an x-ray on a light box, rather than judging by surface impressions.

The collaboration with Kaspersky is the focus of the second part. Shok-1 normally works with spray paint, but because Kaspersky is a technology company, he wanted to make this piece using only technology, built around real medical equipment. He describes how the source x-ray is a utilitarian image made for a doctor's diagnosis, and how much of the work goes into transforming it into something that can stand as an artwork in its own right. The piece was designed in Akihabara and Tokyo, where neon and sci-fi influences shaped its look. He compares the neon lights over a dark sky to the energy of the city.

He closes by linking the work to a world of confusing, fake information, where it is hard to know who to believe and what to trust. In his view, making a subject fully transparent is a crucial step on the road to the truth.

talks.title: Why should you care about stalkerware
talks.teaser: Explains why stalkerware harms people beyond the wealthy and urges antivirus vendors to flag it as malicious.
talks.summary:
Eva Galperin, director of cybersecurity at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, opens by arguing that control of someone's phone is nearly as revealing as access to their thoughts. She explains how her work on this issue started: a survivor of assault by a fellow researcher told her she had stayed silent because he could break into her devices. Galperin responded by offering forensic analysis to people in similar situations, and the requests that followed have continued.

The middle of the talk covers the range of people who reach out to her. One person had children taken during a bitter divorce. Another woman learned that a former partner had been watching her through an internet-connected thermostat. A man was outed as gay to his very conservative family. Galperin stresses that these victims are rarely the customers security vendors picture, since they often lack money, institutional backing or control over their own finances.

She argues that there is no legitimate purpose for software built to run covertly and to convince the device owner that nothing is wrong. She asks antivirus companies to take the threat seriously and to label spouseware and stalkerware as malicious. She also notes that spying on a partner is often illegal, and she encourages the security community to call out these tools whenever they find them and to imagine themselves as potential victims.

The talk, given at an industrial security conference, tackles a common problem: technical staff struggle to win support from executives and boards for security work. The speaker, an industrial control systems consultant with decades of experience across utilities, oil and gas, and mining, argues that executives worry more about losing money than about being hacked. Executives tend to accept more risk than security teams, trust outside voices more than internal staff, and shut down when they feel scared or criticised.

The middle of the talk covers preparation. Presenters should research the company's ownership, lines of business and supply chain, then frame a security issue as a business risk. Useful measures include revenue loss, the cost of an outage per minute, insurance, regulation and market shifts. Root cause analysis and proof from similar companies carry weight, while fear tactics backfire. Plain terms such as risk reduction, continuity and operational efficiency work better than jargon, and one-page stoplight charts help. Speakers should present bookend options with the preferred one in the middle, and set a decision deadline, since no decision means accepting the risk.

The closing example proposes a monitoring project for ICS assets, branded as visible operations and justified by uptime, lower maintenance costs, reuse of existing networks and a phased rollout. The takeaway is that a security professional's role is to help the business make money safely, staying calm and matter-of-fact, and returning later if a decision is deferred.

talks.title: Rootkit Detection and Removal
talks.teaser: Shows how an endpoint security product detects and removes rootkits that hide from classic antivirus scanners.
talks.summary:
The demo shows how Kaspersky Endpoint Security for Business finds and removes rootkits, which hide malicious code and activity from traditional antivirus software. The test machine is first left unprotected so the samples can run. Several malware samples are started and set to launch from the registry autorun, imitating a persistent infection. A special tool then applies common concealment methods: one sample is blocked from being read, scanned or deleted by other processes, while other samples and registry entries are hidden until they become unreadable or invisible.

With protection switched on, a critical areas scan that includes autorun checks flags the rootkit. The administrator then chooses a stronger mode combining system blocking with guaranteed rootkit disinfection, which requires a reboot. After the restart, the planted components are checked across all the locations where they were placed and have been removed. The product log records every detection and removal, and each entry can be opened to see the individual malicious component. A second critical areas scan finds no remaining rootkits or threats.

The takeaway is that a standard scan can miss rootkits that conceal themselves, so a dedicated anti-rootkit component is needed to reach hidden code. Removal may also depend on a reboot to finish cleaning up. Repeating a scan afterwards is a simple way to confirm the system is clean.

talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Is Advanced Endpoint Security a commodity for Business?.
talks.summary:
### Overview
The presentation explores modern endpoint cybersecurity challenges, questioning the traditional two-pronged strategy where basic tools handle mass threats while separate advanced solutions tackle complex, targeted attacks. In large-scale enterprise environments safeguarding tens of thousands of endpoints, even a 0.1% breach rate is critical. As cyber attacks continually evolve, traditional tools fall short, necessitating integrated platforms that span all levels of protection to counter targeted and advanced threats.

### Key Topics
- Limitations of two-pronged and traditional security approaches when managing thousands of endpoints.
- The criticality of small threat margins (e.g., 0.1% unhandled threats) in modern digital environments.
- Unifying threat categories and protection layers through advanced endpoint security platforms.
- Machine learning and artificial intelligence integration for real-time, global threat neutralization.

### Technical Details
The presentation highlights Kaspersky Endpoint Security, framed as a new-generation platform designed to counter current and future threats:
- **Architecture and Deployment**: Operates across physical, virtual, and mobile endpoints (including workstations and critical servers) without demanding changes to existing corporate infrastructure or processes.
- **Core Capabilities**: Detects and halts malicious object delivery, governs application execution, and rolls back systems to their pre-infected states.
- **Behavioral & Correlation Analysis**: Analyzes objects at all protection stages on an additional meta-layer, exposing complex correlations among events and behavioral patterns to construct full threat context.
- **Machine Learning & AI Cloud Integration**: Leverages machine learning algorithms alongside a unified, AI-driven global threat database. Threat intelligence updates instantaneously and automatically across all connected enterprises whenever a new threat attempts an attack anywhere on the network.
- **Reliability**: Engineered to neutralize threats without generating false positives, with validation cited from industry analysts, independent test laboratories, and customers.

### Takeaways
- Relying on separate basic tools for mass threats and advanced tools for targeted attacks leaves vulnerabilities that become significant at scale.
- Effective modern defense requires breaking down boundaries between threat categories with an integrated endpoint platform.
- Automated, cloud-synchronized threat intelligence sharing ensures that defense against an attack on one enterprise immediately shields all other network participants.

talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Endpoint Detection and Response: Reduce Costs without Scrimping on Protection.
talks.summary:
Overview
This talk addresses the financial and operational challenges of manual incident management and presents Kaspersky Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) as a solution to automate incident response while maintaining protection against advanced threats.

Key Challenge
The speaker cites a striking statistic: 52% of companies struggle to distinguish significant security incidents from those that can lead to advanced persistent threats (APTs). Manual gathering, analysis, and validation of incidents is expensive, time-consuming, and requires specialized expertise. Cyberattacks cost businesses between $456,000 and $1.2 million on average, with costs doubling if detection and mitigation fail. This has made cybersecurity a top management priority amid widespread digital transformation.

Incident Management Workflow
The speaker outlines the ideal incident management process in five stages:
1. Data Collection—gathering user and application activity data across the network
2. Visualization & Monitoring—presenting raw data in meaningful context for security specialists
3. Incident Detection—using either threat hunting (manual/semi-automated, leveraging indicators of compromise and expert judgment) or automated detection (combining sandboxing and machine learning)
4. Validation—distinguishing harmless issues from genuine threats
5. Response—taking action to prevent or mitigate identified threats

The Manual Process Problem
When executed manually, this workflow overwhelms IT teams. Many organizations get stuck at steps 1–3 and lack resources to proceed to validation and response, leaving threats unaddressed.

Kaspersky EDR Solution
Kaspersky Endpoint Detection and Response automates the first two workflow steps, freeing IT specialists to focus on critical validation and response work. The solution combines five core elements: monitoring, aggregation, detection, response, and prevention. Built on 20 years of expertise, it operates as an on-premises solution for privacy compliance, integrates with existing endpoint protection (including third-party solutions), and requires no additional software if Kaspersky Endpoint Security for Business is already deployed.

Key Takeaways
Endpoint Detection and Response reduces costs without compromising protection by automating security processes, lowering advanced threat risk, eliminating the need for additional IT staff, and optimizing the capabilities of existing security teams. The solution helps prevent business disruption from advanced threats.

talks.title: Cyber Pulse: The State of Cybersecurity in Healthcare
talks.teaser: Part 2 explores Cyber Pulse: The State of Cybersecurity in Healthcare.
talks.summary:
### Overview
With information-sharing systems proliferating across healthcare environments, safeguarding sensitive patient data has become critical. As of January 2019, over 200 US healthcare organizations suffered IT or hacking-related incidents that affected 500 or more patients. Breached healthcare providers face significant recovery costs, spending an average of $408 per patient to recover healthcare records and up to $1.7 million in advertising to address reputational damage. To explore the factors driving these issues, Kaspersky commissioned a survey of nearly 2,000 healthcare employees across the United States and Canada, evaluating regulatory awareness, security policies, training, and device security protection.

### Key Topics
- **Regulatory Awareness:** Longstanding frameworks exist—such as HIPAA instituted in 1996 in the US and PIPEDA/PIPA in 2000 in Canada—yet organizations struggle to make staff aware of compliance mandates.
- **Security Policies & Governance:** The necessity of establishing and communicating clear cybersecurity policies so staff understand their role in incident prevention and mitigation.
- **Cybersecurity Training:** Developing a culture of vigilance where personnel receive initial and recurrent training on identifying threats and handling security incidents.
- **Device Protection & IT Awareness:** Visibility into how IT systems and endpoint devices storing protected health information (PHI) are secured.

### Technical Details
- **Regulatory Gaps:** 18% of surveyed US healthcare workers did not know the meaning of the HIPAA Security Rule. In Canada, where British Columbia and Nova Scotia prohibit storing protected health information in the US, 49% of Canadian healthcare respondents did not know where PHI had to reside.
- **Policy Deficits:** 21% of respondents were unaware of any cybersecurity policy within their organization while acknowledging one should exist. Among organizations with policies, only 17% of employees in medium and enterprise organizations and 10% in smaller organizations reported reading it more than once.
- **Training Shortfalls:** Approximately one-third of US healthcare employees reported never receiving cybersecurity training despite acknowledging they should have, and roughly one-fifth expressed a need for more training. Comparing employee populations, 24% of US respondents and 41% of Canadian respondents had never received cybersecurity training.
- **Device Security Visibility:** 40% of surveyed healthcare staff did not know how their IT devices were protected. Unawareness was inversely correlated with organization size: 53% of employees in small organizations were unaware of device protections, compared to 39% in medium organizations and 36% in large enterprise organizations.

### Takeaways
Healthcare organizations must improve education regarding regulatory requirements, general security awareness, and incident response protocols so workers know how to respond to suspected issues. Furthermore, healthcare providers must not only implement technical controls on systems storing patient data, but actively communicate these protections to staff to ensure organizational adherence and cultivate employee confidence in data protection practices.

The speaker opens with a condensed version of a longer talk, arguing that the internet has changed information warfare in a fundamental way. Historically, an operator needed someone who knew the target audience intimately, had grown up with it, and could devise messages that would resonate. That insider is no longer required, because engagement metrics such as likes show almost immediately whether an operation is landing. If it is not working, the operator can drop it and try something else, so the key shift is feedback rather than expertise, and people without deep specialist knowledge can run these campaigns effectively.

The speaker also describes their own research path: about fifteen years of technical work, followed by roughly five years on softer subjects such as espionage, terrorism, information warfare, hiding secrets and investigations. The rest of the clip is informal remarks about being at this conference for the first time. They praise the friendly staff, the large and elaborate stage setup, and the strong mix of speakers, and they say the audience has a good number of technically capable people without too many uninteresting attendees.

For a practitioner, the main takeaway is that influence campaigns now depend less on cultural insight and more on measuring audience response and iterating quickly. Defenders who only look for expert-crafted narratives may miss operations that are built by trial and error from public engagement data.

talks.title: Part 2: How to connect computers and mobile devices
talks.teaser: Shows how computers and mobile devices are invited, installed and registered in a Kaspersky Endpoint Security Cloud workspace.
talks.summary:
This walkthrough covers onboarding computers and phones into a Kaspersky Endpoint Security Cloud workspace. An administrator sends invitations, and each recipient clicks one universal link that detects the operating system and sends the device to the matching installer. Installation needs administrative rights on the device but no decisions from the user. On macOS, the product follows the system interface language and receives its license once it reaches the cloud service.

Android phones running version 4.2 or later are handled through the Play Store. If the invitation cannot be opened on the phone, the user can scan a QR code shown in the message on a computer. After the app is installed, its setup wizard asks for permissions to scan files and apps, to act as device administrator for remote wipe and lock, to locate the device and use its camera, and to run as an accessibility service for better phishing protection. Samsung devices also need approval for Knox integration. The app then gets its license, updates signatures and scans the device. Sync runs every six hours by default, but push messages through Firebase Cloud Messaging deliver new settings or commands within seconds. Portable devices receive owners automatically, or an administrator assigns them manually.

Windows installation uses the same package, downloaded from the workspace or an invitation, and installs the endpoint product together with the network agent. The presenter notes that the process matches what happens on server systems. Computers have no owners by default and use the default security profile. Owners only need to be assigned when different groups require different security profiles.

talks.teaser: Introduces a course on protecting small networks with Kaspersky Endpoint Security Cloud and explains who should use it.
talks.summary:
This introductory lesson opens a course on protecting small companies, imagined as a network of about 250 computers and mobile devices running Windows, macOS, Android or iOS. The course centres on Kaspersky Endpoint Security Cloud, a security-as-a-service product whose administration console is hosted by the vendor rather than installed on the company's own servers. The product draws on components from Kaspersky Endpoint Security for Business, but offers a trimmed set suited to modest networks.

The presenter compares the vendor's options for small businesses. Kaspersky Small Office Security, with its web console, fits networks of roughly five to 25 devices that have no dedicated administrator. Endpoint Security for Business gives full protection with no device cap, but depends on an on-premises Security Center server that requires a skilled administrator. Endpoint Security Cloud sits between these: it allows up to 999 devices per workspace, licenses are counted per user across one computer and two mobile devices, and it comes in Standard and Plus editions from version 8.0 onward.

Likely users include administrators of small single-site networks, geographically spread offices without an obvious headquarters, and managed service providers who run separate companies from one console. Through the console, administrators can add devices, apply configuration profiles to groups, run scans and updates, read event notifications and reports, manage licenses, and on Android locate, lock or wipe a lost phone. The course then covers signing up, connecting devices, configuring protection and post-setup tasks.
