talks.summary:
Kaspersky security evangelist David looks at whether student grades can really be hacked. Searching the dark web, he found stolen diplomas and certificates, along with sellers offering to change grades for students at particular schools. He also reviewed vulnerabilities in popular school software that could expose sensitive information, but concluded that these flaws are probably not the usual route into such systems.

In his view, the most common way school portals get broken into is through reused passwords. Because students and staff often choose their own passwords, one leaked credential can give an attacker access to an account. He recommends that schools, teachers and parents review their passwords and turn on two-factor authentication wherever the portal supports it, and that they check whether a child's grades look right.

For IT staff, he suggests network segmentation so that school management systems are not on the same network as students. He also advises searching public dark web marketplaces for listings tied to your own school. He closes with a short message to students: do not hack your school.

talks.title: Zebrocy’s Multi-Language Malware Salad: Kurt Baumgartner at
talks.teaser: Traces the Zebrocy group's spearphishing campaigns, its multi-language implants, and its links to Sofacy and BlackEnergy.
talks.summary:
Kurt Baumgartner of Kaspersky's global research team profiles Zebrocy, a Russian-speaking group that has run spearphishing waves against hundreds of targets since late 2015. Its operators profile victims, steal credentials and keep access quietly. He places the group as a subset of the Sofacy lineage, pointing to shared infrastructure and to a custom RC4 routine and API hashing that appeared in Delphi and BlackEnergy kernel loaders until about 2015.

The talk then follows the malware through its languages: AutoIt droppers in 2015, Delphi backdoors, .NET modules from 2017, and Go implants more recently, with cryptography modules added over time. Each campaign collects a volume serial number, system information, a process list and a screenshot. Second-stage implants are chosen according to which browsers and mail clients appear in that process list. Other modules steal files from network drives and removable media, log keystrokes, and harvest credentials from email clients. Baumgartner also notes that the group copies portions of public code and recompiles them for each target.

He checks his earlier predictions against the data, including a surge of activity in late 2018 and the disappearance of the Sofacy SPLM implant from the targets he tracked. For 2019 he expects more spearphishing, possible use of Python or Ruby, and continued credential theft, and he raises machine-learning-guided development as a possible reason for the rapid code changes. The takeaway is that the group's per-target variants and focus on credentials and quiet persistence make mailbox and browser credential monitoring important.

talks.summary:
This session is a startup pitch review. The founders have built a product that embeds a small NFC tag in luxury and fashion items during manufacturing. Shoppers tap the item with a phone app to check authenticity, see whether it is worth buying, and unlock exclusive content. The main problem is distribution. Selling directly to brands is slow, large luxury houses have long deal cycles and avoid being first, and six months of effort produced little result.

The team is shifting toward smaller brands and considering agencies and consultancies as channel partners. Their revenue-sharing program started at a 20% commission, rose to 50%, and they are weighing a further increase. The advisor recommends starting with a much higher margin, citing successful reseller networks that give partners 80 to 90 percent to win early references and success stories, then revising terms annually as the business grows. The advisor also suggests framing the pitch around the vendor's own goals, such as real-time inventory visibility, rather than only consumer benefits, because direct sales conversion is limited when buyers decide in several steps.

For marketing, the advice is to invest in branding and educational content, such as practical guides on spotting genuine products, quizzes and engagement features, and to grow a channel audience. The advisor also recommends reserving budget to build an early adopter community, distributing the product to consumers, and offering exclusive content, since real users demonstrating the product is more persuasive than vendor claims. The session ends with an agreement to review progress in a couple of months.

talks.title: Not why, but when: how to get prepared to deal with data breaches
talks.teaser: Outlines three preparation steps for a data breach: technical response, public communication and legal obligations.
talks.summary:
The speaker reframes the usual question after a data breach. The useful question is not why it happened but when an organisation will be ready for it. Breaches usually trace back to weak data management and the lack of a real cyber security strategy, and they can start from many sources, such as a recently dismissed employee, an outside attacker, or a curious person who finds exposed data through a public search. Rather than dwelling on causes, the talk focuses on the response.

The first step is technical. The security team should establish a clear picture of what happened and carry out incident response and remediation, bringing in an outside partner if the company cannot handle it alone. The second step is communication. The company should agree in advance what is said internally and to the public, avoiding panic and avoiding making the situation worse. Remediation comes first, so that later messages to customers, partners, consumers and suppliers rest on solid facts.

The third step is the legal position. Teams should check whether any rules were broken, noting that GDPR applies in Europe and similar regulations are spreading in other regions. The company needs to know what it must do, and what its responsibility and liability are if a regulation was violated. The closing message is that a breach response plan is best built before an incident happens.

The proposed fix is to automate the process for these small accounts, so distributors spend less time and money on them and can focus on more valuable work. talks.title: Save The World, Fast with D*Face
talks.teaser: A street artist explains how passing thoughts become murals and digital work, and why speed needs preparation.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This talk features artist D*Face (Dean Stockton), who reflects on his identity as a hybrid artist whose work spans illustration, graphic design, graffiti, and contemporary art. He discusses his creative process, his view of digital technology as an artistic tool, his background with motorcycle culture, and his collaboration with cybersecurity company Kaspersky Lab to inspire the public and encourage social change.

### Key Topics
- **Artistic Identity and Idea Generation:** Stockton describes art as being defined by the person creating it. His own work sits at the intersection of illustration, graphic design, graffiti, and contemporary art. Ideas typically originate as fleeting thoughts, words, or sentences captured on his phone or a bedside notebook upon waking up or drifting off to sleep.
- **Subculture and Community:** He references "rubbers Alliance" (Rebels Alliance), describing it as a motorcycle community focused on lifestyle, culture, and customization.
- **Digital Tools and Traditional Mediums:** Stockton emphasizes that working digitally is a fundamental element of his workflow. He treats computers not as a replacement for traditional methods, but as another essential tool—akin to a "magic pencil" or a pen in a sketchbook—among a plethora of equipment he relies on.
- **Studio vs. Street Art:** Reflecting on two decades of leaving his mark worldwide through murals and stickers, Stockton highlights the differences between studio creation on a computer screen and painting on a street wall. Each medium offers distinct aesthetic qualities and graces that cannot be replicated by the other.
- **The Mural Concept:** The concept behind his mural explores the fast pace of life, memory, and recollection, combining recognizable individual features into a fresh, cohesive composition.
- **Speed, Safety, and Collaboration:** The speaker highlights the relationship between speed and safety, noting that speed requires preparation and avoiding unnecessary risks. He notes his partnership with Kaspersky Lab, highlighting their shared goal of bringing art to the public to make a positive statement and inspire social change.

### Technical Details
Note: The transcript contains minimal cybersecurity technical depth or vulnerability disclosures, as the talk focuses primarily on visual design, artistic techniques, and creative collaboration.
- **Workflow & Tooling:** Stockton relies on computers alongside traditional pens and sketchbooks to draft visuals before transferring them onto physical walls.
- **Safety Concept:** The talk parallels the necessity of safety and preparation when moving fast, contrasting reckless risk-taking with disciplined preparedness.

### Takeaways
- Technology functions as an augmenting tool in creative production rather than replacing physical craft.
- Speed in execution requires intentional preparation and risk mitigation rather than careless haste.
- Cross-disciplinary partnerships, such as the artist's collaboration with Kaspersky Lab, can serve as a medium to reach the public, provoke thought, and inspire social change.

talks.title: Can software keep your pets safe?
talks.teaser: Shows a smart home configured to keep pets safe from garage doors, open gates, window falls and tank failures.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Oleg Zaytsev, an expert at Kaspersky Lab, shares how he designed and automated his Smart Home with pet safety and comfort as core design requirements. Addressing hazards faced by various domestic animals—including unleashed dogs, cats, turtles, and aquarium fish—the presentation demonstrates how consumer IoT, surveillance scripting, and automated fail-safes can mitigate domestic risks.

### Key Topics
- **Automated Protection for Roaming Pets:** Addressing risks for unleashed dogs such as escaping through open entrance gates, getting crushed by garage doors, or getting struck by reversing vehicles.
- **Event-Driven Video Surveillance:** Deploying video cameras capable of running event scripts (e.g., motion detection) to detect animals—such as a Yorkshire Terrier or intruder animals like a neighbor's cat—and feeding telemetry into the central control system.
- **Aquarium and Terrarium Environment Controls:** Managing water conditions, heating, filtration, lighting, and leak detection for fish and turtles, supported by independent fail-safes.
- **Home Climate vs. Fall Hazards:** Eliminating the danger of cats falling from heights by relying on forced air ventilation instead of opening windows.

### Technical Details
- **Access Restriction Mechanism:** A dedicated smartphone-activated mode ('Dog on premises' in the 'Unleashed dog' section) places automated locks on motorized barriers. When an attempt is made to open or close the garage door while this restriction is active, the Smart Home blocks the command and outputs an audible voice alert.
- **Surveillance Scripting:** Standard surveillance cameras are configured to execute scripts upon motion detection, passing pet movements and intruder alerts directly to the Smart Home control center.
- **Fail-Safe Aquarium Safeguards:** The aquarium system monitors water pumps, filters, and temperature. Secondary protection systems operate independently to prevent abnormal conditions, such as overheating, even if the primary Smart Home automation malfunctions. (Automated feeders are intentionally omitted to preserve human-pet interaction).
- **Turtle Tank Leak Response:** When a leak sensor activates, the Smart Home issues voice announcements throughout the house, sends SMS and email notifications, automatically disables water heaters and filters, and logs the incident on the management screen until manually reset via an 'All clear' button.

### Takeaways
Designing smart home automation requires striking a deliberate balance between convenience, comfort, and security. By integrating responsive sensor scripts, hardware interlocks, multi-channel alerting, and independent fail-safes, automation software can effectively protect pets from household accidents.

talks.title: What it is, what it’s not, and what you need to do
talks.teaser: Explains what GDPR is and is not, and outlines cybersecurity measures that support compliance with it.
talks.summary:
The talk explains the EU General Data Protection Regulation by first setting out what it is not. GDPR is not a checklist that a company can satisfy by adding a few tools and processes. It applies beyond the EU itself, reaching EU companies that hold data on non-citizens and non-EU firms that offer products to people in the EU. It also does not prescribe how to build secure processes, so organisations must decide their own approach and accept that incidents may be judged as failures, even when they believe they acted correctly.

The speaker then describes GDPR as an ongoing process aimed at giving people real control over their personal data and ensuring that companies use and secure that data lawfully. It clarifies the responsibilities of data controllers and data processors, and it requires regular assessment and adjustment. Cybersecurity is presented as one of the cornerstones of compliance, though strong security alone does not equal compliance. The practical measures covered include protecting endpoints, including mobile devices, encrypting data at rest and in transit, securing regulated storage, and adding protection at the gateway and email server to reduce human error.

The talk closes by recommending regular penetration tests and security assessments so that weaknesses are found before attackers find them. Knowing what happens across the infrastructure is also key, because after a breach, the ability to establish the cause helps reduce risk and shows that reasonable efforts were made to protect data. The core takeaway for practitioners is that the underlying obligation is to protect the data.

talks.title: THE HARDWARE PIVOT
talks.teaser: Shows how cheap hardware implants can serve as a first step toward software compromise in targeted attacks.
talks.summary:
Joe FitzPatrick opens by challenging the common belief that hardware attacks are too difficult, too expensive or only a concern for nation states. He argues that physical access is a low barrier, that commodity parts make implants practical, and that hardware is hard for most people to inspect, which is why it gets underestimated.

He then walks through examples. A counterfeit Cisco switch had extra headers soldered on to unlock all of its ports. The leaked ANT catalog included Cottonmouth, a USB cable with a radio that relayed data from a compromised system. A charging cable sold for about $7 can hide a GSM module and SIM slot, allowing a caller to open a microphone or get the device's location from cell towers. A $5 programmable Bluetooth module can log nearby device addresses. Board-level implants, such as an open-source JTAG device and a PCI Express DMA board, can persist on a server past wiping. He also explains why air-gapped networks, heavily monitored environments, supply chains and social engineering make hardware attractive.

The core idea is a pivot: use physical access to place a hardware implant, use it to gain software privilege, then carry out the rest of the work in software, which scales far better than building thousands of devices. He suggests this fits red team engagements and penetration tests, where physical techniques such as dumping firmware can inform later software attacks. The practical takeaway is that hardware is not magic, its skills are learnable or can be outsourced, and organisations should not dismiss it as a threat.

talks.title: MASHA AND THESE BEARS
talks.teaser: Traces how the APT28 group shifted its malware, infrastructure and targeting toward Asia during 2018.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Kurt, a principal security researcher on Kaspersky's Global Research and Analysis Team (GReAT), analyzes significant shifts in the operations of the threat group APT28 (also referred to as Sofacy) heading into 2018. While historically known for Western-focused operations such as targeting NATO, Ukraine, European elections, and the DNC hack, Sofacy has evolved into a more agile and measured actor. Kurt highlights key evolutions in their toolset, infrastructure, development culture, and geographic targeting, specifically their movement further east into Asia.

### Key Topics
- **Targeting Pivot to the Far East**: Moving beyond historical Western targets and Central Asian "-stans", Sofacy expanded operations across Mongolia, Japan, and China in 2018.
- **Target Overlap with Gray Lambert**: A notable compromise occurred on an aerospace and defense conglomerate server in China previously infected with Gray Lambert (a user-mode passive sniffer implant associated with the Lambert actor family).
- **Decline of SPLM / X-Agent**: The traditional heavy C++ backdoor known as SPLM or CHOPSTICK is largely disappearing from active deployments, replaced by smaller in-memory modules and new frameworks.
- **Rise of Zebrocy**: A subgroup of Sofacy utilizing modular .NET and PowerShell tools, distinct IP-based infrastructure, and rapidly iterating codebases.

### Technical Details
- **Malware Evolution**: Historically, Sofacy maintained consistent C++ codebases over long periods (2004–2009 and 2009–2015). By 2017–2018, the ~300 KB fully featured SPLM backdoor—which bundled keyloggers, remote shells, and file-stealing capabilities communicating over HTTP, FTP, or SMTP—fell out of widespread use. In 2018, SPLM appeared almost exclusively as small in-memory remote shell modules.
- **Chinese Server Overlap**: Sofacy deployed in-memory components onto a Chinese aerospace server shortly after Kaspersky cleaned up Gray Lambert. Hypothesized infection vectors include shared vulnerable web application exploitation (most likely), replay of recorded Lambert magic-value sessions, Lambert false flags, or stolen Sofacy tooling.
- **Cryptography Comparison**: Sofacy's 2017 in-memory plugins use a custom 32-round feedback-based cipher recompiled per victim with changing operators and constraints (distinct from NSA's Speck algorithm). In 2016 (DNC hack), they used simpler sequential XOR operations. In contrast, threat group Turla demonstrates professional standard cryptography (RSA, DES, 3DES) coupled with immature commentary, while Zebrocy implements simpler, practical custom crypto routines.
- **Zebrocy Characteristics**: Zebrocy relies on .NET and PowerShell rather than C++, incorporating USB/removable drive monitoring to exfiltrate files and borrowing open-source tooling such as PowerShell Empire. Zebrocy also utilizes configuration INI files with build ID formatting reminiscent of BlackEnergy's 2014 custom plugins.
- **Infrastructure Shifts**: Traditional Sofacy infrastructure relied on domain names registered via privacy services and paid using Bitcoin. Zebrocy and newer operations have moved toward bare IP addresses, eliminating the need for domain anonymity services.

### Takeaways
Into 2018 and beyond, Sofacy operations demonstrate heightened agility. Defenders must anticipate continuing abandonment of legacy C++ code in favor of modular .NET, PowerShell, and open-source frameworks, continued diversification away from domain-centric infrastructure toward IP-based command-and-control, and broadened geographic targeting across East Asia.

talks.teaser: Traces the Dark Caracal espionage campaign from phishing lures to its mobile and desktop malware families.
talks.summary:
This talk introduces Dark Caracal, a threat actor the researchers have tracked since around 2016, when phishing emails aimed at a Kazakh journalist's organisation revealed a wider campaign against dissidents, lawyers and opposition figures. The first part explains how the researchers connected a mobile component to infrastructure already reported, and how victims were reached through WhatsApp messages, a fake app store and social media lures.

The mobile samples were trojanized versions of secure messengers, Tor and a circumvention VPN. They kept their normal features while quietly adding surveillance: call and ambient audio recording, text interception, location tracking, Wi-Fi scanning and remote command execution. One sample pulled from a command server was linked to the commercial FinFisher toolkit, suggesting the actor first used bought tooling before writing its own. On the desktop side, the speakers showed macro-laden documents and a compiled help file that launched PowerShell, followed by Bandook, a modular Windows RAT injected into a legitimate process, and Cross RAT, a newly seen cross-platform Java implant.

The main takeaway is that this group needed no zero-day exploits. Convincing messages and largely public code were enough to compromise targets, so defenders should not focus only on high-profile exploit chains. Attribution and the infrastructure behind the campaign were deferred to the second half of the presentation.

The video opens with the risk of losing an Android device to malware or theft and presents a short list of protective habits. Viewers are advised to install apps only from the official Google Play store, check a developer's background, read reviews critically, and look at install counts. The presenter also recommends scrutinizing the permissions an app requests, since a game has no reason to read stored files or access contacts. Unused apps should be removed, because they can still run activity in the background.

The next part covers updates and account protection. Keeping the operating system and apps current closes known security holes. Two-factor authentication is recommended for email, social media and banking accounts, so that a stolen password alone is not enough to log in. A long PIN or passphrase is preferred over a pattern lock, which is easy to spot on a screen. Online shopping and banking should be avoided on public Wi-Fi, or done through a VPN that encrypts the connection.

The video closes with tools for when something goes wrong. A mobile anti-malware app, free or paid, adds basic defense, and app locking can guard banking and other sensitive apps. Anti-theft features can sound an alarm, photograph the person holding the phone, lock the device and wipe its data remotely. The presenter concludes that security depends mostly on awareness and only partly on technology.

talks.teaser: Panelists weigh whether security risk can be accepted, how insurance fits alongside controls, and how to manage supplier data risk.
talks.summary:
The panel opens with a question about whether organisations can simply tolerate risk and handle the fallout afterwards. The panelists agree that accepting risk is a business decision rather than a security one, and that the security chief's role is to give leadership information and opinion. Security has to be weighed against financial, legal, cultural and people risks, and firms first need to know where their critical data sits and what the business actually does.

Discussion then turns to insurance and smaller companies. One panelist argues that insurance should complement good controls rather than replace them, noting that policies differ in coverage and excess, and that insurers can supply incident response, legal and forensic help that small firms rarely have on retainer. Another recalls a claim from an optician whose three branches stopped trading after ransomware, showing that data now drives the business more than the hardware does. Small firms often feel they have nothing worth protecting, yet data is their most sought-after asset.

Later sections cover encryption, supply chains and hiring. Panelists say full disk encryption is becoming invisible, but teams must also check data in databases, cloud services and network traffic. For suppliers, they recommend tiering checks by data sensitivity, building working relationships, and cutting bloated questionnaires, since a shorter form often produces more usable answers. The closing theme is talent: degree and certification barriers should fall, because some strong red-team candidates lack polished social skills.

talks.title: What is Spyware?
talks.teaser: Explains what spyware is, how it reaches devices, and the damage it can cause to personal data.
talks.summary:
## Overview
This educational video explains what spyware is and its threat landscape. Spyware is defined as software designed to gather data from a device and communicate personal and confidential information to malicious actors. The presentation emphasizes that any device connected to the Internet is at risk of spyware infestation.

## Infection Methods
The transcript identifies four primary ways spyware infects devices:
1. **Trojans and Social Engineering**: Spyware disguised as legitimate software, using social engineering tactics to trick users into executing malicious code.
2. **Bundled with Legitimate Programs**: Exploitation of user interactions with adware, freeware, and riskyware, as well as interactions with advertisements and adult content.
3. **Tracking Cookies**: Compromised tracking cookies commonly employed by websites.
4. **System Monitors**: Tools designed to monitor computer activity and performance that can be exploited.

## Consequences of Infection
Once installed, spyware causes significant damage:
- **Data Theft**: Compromises email activity, passwords, social media accounts, credit card information, and purchase history; threatens online identity and enables imitation fraud.
- **Performance Degradation**: Consumes device resources, causing slowness, application crashes, and overheating.
- **Malicious Redirection**: Manipulates search results and displays fraudulent websites that trick users into further infections.

## Prevention and Mitigation
The video recommends a layered defense approach:
- **Safe Browsing Practices**: Avoid clicking unexpected email links and suspicious websites.
- **Security Solutions**: Use trusted internet security software for early detection and proactive protection.
- **Removal Tools**: Deploy spyware removal tools for already-infected devices to identify and eliminate threats.

## Takeaways
Spyware poses multifaceted threats combining data theft, privacy violation, and system compromise. Prevention through vigilant browsing and professional security tools remains the most practical defense strategy.

talks.title: HARDENING ANDROID AGAINST RANSOMWARE, ONE DESSERT AT A TIME
talks.teaser: Explains how recent Android platform changes limit ransomware's ability to block screens, persist on devices, and damage data.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a malware analyst on Google's Android security team, explains that ransomware breaks several of Android's core rules: it blocks the device, encrypts user data, and resists removal. Ransomware has appeared on Android since around 2014, with roughly 30 families tracked. The talk examines which legitimate APIs these apps abuse and how the platform has responded.

The talk walks through the changes release by release. Apps once used the running-tasks API, and later the proc directory, to find the foreground app. Lollipop deprecated the first route and Nougat hid process data in the second. Overlay windows of the system alert type could sit above everything, including the keyguard. Android O replaces them with a floating layer and places older window types below important system layers. For persistence, about 70 percent of ransomware used device admin privileges. Nougat added an uninstall option to the device admin prompt, removed the option that let an app block its own disabling, and allowed forced removal from the app list. Storage access was narrowed to granular media and document types in Nougat, which limits damage from encryption. Runtime permission prompts from Marshmallow let users deny collateral-damage permissions such as SMS, camera, and location.

The speaker notes that cloud photo, music, and backup services give users a way to recover from data loss. For devices that have not updated, Google's app verification service now permanently blocks all known ransomware rather than only warning about some types. The takeaway is that platform hardening is slow and continuous, and that researchers should report ransomware that gets past verification.

talks.summary:
The talk casts IT as a fast-moving monkey that chases new products and OT as a cautious elephant that must stay up around the clock. It opens with a playful history of industrial control, from an 18th-century experiment with electricity to Charles Babbage's unfinished engines, and then moves to the consequences of this clash.

The speaker walks through three sets of incidents. A December 2015 attack on a power company knocked about 30 substations offline for three hours, and operators restored them by switching manually after the intruders entered through a phishing email. A later outage in Kyiv is raised as a possible sign that such attacks are repeating. A water utility case, presented under a fictional name, shows an AS/400 that ran both plant control and corporate IT, database credentials stored in clear text on a payment web server, and a single staff member who could operate the system. Finally, the Shamoon wiper attack on Saudi Aramco erased about 35,000 computers, forcing a return to paper and faxes while recovery took months and tens of thousands of hard drives.

The closing section turns to Internet of Things devices, where the speaker points to tight cost targets that leave security as an afterthought, the difficulty of patching hardware in the field, and a widening gap between device counts and security maturity. Suggested remedies are simpler code with fewer features, awareness among end users, developers and management, and regular knowledge exchange between experts, with a monthly meeting proposed as a joke. The talk ends with a skit in which the monkey and the elephant are taken over by a rival.

talks.teaser: Panelists debate breach disclosure timing, GDPR reporting, staff awareness and how to frame cyber risk for boards.
talks.summary:
A panel of industry practitioners discusses the enterprise risks organisations face and how to reduce them. The opening question is whether the human problem can ever be fixed. The panelists agree technology alone cannot solve it and argue that awareness should be continuous and tailored to individuals, rather than an annual course. They criticise phishing exercises that track click rates without changing behaviour.

Much of the debate centres on breach disclosure. Speakers caution against announcing figures before they are confirmed, citing TalkTalk, which initially said up to four million customers could be affected, a number later revised sharply down. Under GDPR, an initial notice is due within 72 hours, but panelists said regulators accept phased updates if the organisation appears in control. In the Sony attack, network sabotage, leaked staff data and extortion demands arrived together, and the company lacked alternative communications. A response tweet from Equifax linked to a phishing site, showing how communication slips can compound a breach.

The panel closes with practical advice. Organisations should plan incident response, including communications, and rehearse it through simulation exercises. They should build relationships with regulators before a crisis and frame risk in terms boards understand, such as share price and executive reputation. Security also belongs in network design from the start, since segmentation bolted on after years of mergers is hard to achieve. Speakers added that staff should be empowered to act, and that organisations should engage the wider research community.

The talk looks at the command-and-control servers behind criminal botnets and automated transfer systems, and at how poorly many of them are built. The speaker, a malware researcher, deployed public panels to study them and walks through the weaknesses found in each case. The opening examples involve an infostealer panel whose login cookies relied on a salt derived from timestamps, making them guessable, and another panel that kept executing code after a redirect, which exposed its data.

The middle section covers upload and file handling flaws. On one Apache setup, a PHP payload slipped past an extension blacklist because Apache walked through multiple file extensions, and a Windows-style extension offered another bypass. Another panel accepted uploaded .htaccess files that mapped a harmless extension to PHP execution. A proxy-level check and a panel-level check could both be defeated. One server exposed its database through an indexing tool with no access control. A transfer system had SQL injection in its login and an accessible SQLite database. On the server side, a root-run binary on a hosting control panel could be hijacked through a manipulable path, a Perl script allowed command injection through crafted file names, and a container escape tied to a user namespace flaw affected a criminal-run hosting service.

The talk closes with access gained through infected botnet operators' own machines, which exposed their logs and wider operations. The main takeaway is that criminal tooling often contains basic mistakes that give researchers visibility into how these groups work. The speaker frames the findings mainly as lessons about how poorly this infrastructure is secured.

The talk examines how easily cheap consumer IoT devices bought from retail sites can be exploited, rather than high-profile products. The speaker, a penetration tester, picked seven devices after a falling-out with some vendors and held three others back under responsible disclosure. The first case is a TP-Link M535 cellular router with a SIM slot, where an SMS sent to the device appears on a web page, so a cross-site scripting payload delivered by text message works even while the device is only switched on.

Other cases follow the same pattern of simple flaws. A retinal scanner checked login in client-side JavaScript, so skipping a status check gave admin or root access. A VStarcam camera had command injection in its FTP settings, a bug described in 2014 that was only partly fixed, and it yielded a root shell. One travel router shipped with a hardcoded root password that users cannot change. Another ran firmware updates through a bash script, where a guest account could reset the admin password. A Trendnet travel router accepted commands through an unauthenticated GET parameter. Finally, a WD MyCloud case involved 85 published flaws, largely parameters fed into commands, with a login bypass among them.

The speaker argues that disclosure breaks down because vendors struggle with many reports, and small researchers end up going public after long email chains. Bug bounty programs or advisory channels that accept findings in one place, with staff who triage them, would help both sides. Researchers and vendors should also talk directly about device architecture.

Kaspersky researchers present three ATM cases from the past year, each handled as a forensic or reverse-engineering job for a bank. The first involves Fess malware, a small DLL that acts only when an operator writes single commands into a text file. Those commands open the dispenser, read cassette data and dispense cash. Because it calls the Microsoft XFS interface, it works with any vendor's ATM, and the attacker reached it through tunnels inside the bank network.

The second case had no cameras or logs, so the team worked from a hard drive and a physical inspection. They found a USB Bluetooth dongle in the cash compartment, paired with a wireless keyboard. The attacker waited about three months for logs to rotate, placed stickers, then rebooted the machine with the keyboard into a Linux service mode that dispensed cash.

The third case involved a man who drilled into an outdoor ATM in daylight, dressed as a construction worker. The researchers decoded the proprietary RS-485 SDC bus, which uses nine-bit encrypted frames at an unknown speed, and mapped device addresses for the printer, screen and dispenser. They derived a dispense equation from test runs, then injected a forged device response carrying a dispense command, since devices trust each other once the controller holds the bus. They built a cheap microcontroller device to reproduce the attack. The lesson is that embedded buses trust their peers, so physical access and bus-level controls matter.

talks.title: A Hunt for the Infamous Hackers to Prevent Large Bank Robberies
talks.teaser: Traces how Kaspersky researchers tracked the Lazarus group across bank intrusions in Asia and Europe.
talks.summary:
In 2016, an anonymous crew took $81 million from the Central Bank of Bangladesh, with a similar attempt reported in Vietnam. Investigators linked the activity to Lazarus, a group active since 2009 that targets manufacturing, media and financial organisations. After months of quiet, a tip-off from an Asian bank sent Kaspersky researchers to the scene, but the intruders had already left, wiping most of their traces.

The talk outlines how Lazarus hits banks. It compromises an internet-facing web system, spreads to other hosts and plants persistent backdoors, then maps the network to find backup and transaction servers. Its final malware issues rogue transfers in the bank's name and relays funds taken from other compromised banks for laundering. Evidence from the Asian case improved detection, and signs of the group soon surfaced worldwide. The attackers built invisible malware, set decoys and disguised their tools, forcing researchers to keep adjusting detection for months.

In January 2017, anomalies at a European bank matched the earlier pattern, and researchers arrived just before a transfer was made. Again the attackers had fled, but this time they left fresh traces to follow. The takeaway is that matching behaviour across incidents and feeding evidence back into detection can expose an actor that works quietly. Kaspersky's products are said to catch all known Lazarus malware.

The video points out that people regularly use public Wi-Fi at coffee shops, hotels and airports, and that data sent over these networks can be intercepted by criminals. A common threat is the fake hotspot, which uses a name similar to a legitimate one. Once a user joins, attackers can watch online activity and look for banking and social media logins. Public connections can also be used to plant viruses and other malicious software, which can damage a device and expose personal information.

Several precautions reduce the risk. Users should confirm the exact network name with staff before connecting, and avoid logging into email, social media or financial accounts on open networks when possible. Turning off file sharing prevents others from reaching files on the device. A VPN encrypts traffic so that an attacker positioned between the user and the connection gains little. Finally, Wi-Fi should be switched off once the user is finished, because the hardware may keep transmitting to nearby networks.

The overall message is that understanding these dangers helps keep important data out of the wrong hands. The video recommends pairing these habits with trusted internet security software.

Ransomware is presented as malware that either locks a computer or phone or encrypts its files until the victim pays a ransom, usually demanded in Bitcoin. The talk uses the Dead Cryptor family as an example, describing a demand of about two Bitcoins, worth more than a thousand dollars. It stresses that ransomware keeps changing with each new modification and is spreading rapidly around the world.

The speaker separates two widely used categories. Locker ransomware blocks basic computer functions until a payment is made, while crypto ransomware encrypts documents and other important files and threatens to destroy them unless a fee is paid. The main infection routes named are spam, spear phishing and watering hole attacks. Scareware is also covered: fake software or alert messages that pose as coming from a legitimate source and then demand payment to restore control of the machine.

For defense, the talk recommends avoiding suspicious emails and links, steering clear of suspicious websites, and learning to recognize scareware tactics. Users should back up their devices and run up-to-date internet security software that includes anti-ransomware features. The central advice is never to pay the ransom, because payment only encourages the criminals behind these scams. The takeaway is that informed habits combined with current protection keep most users safe.

talks.title: Cyber-bullying Facts - Top 10 Forms of Cyber Bullying
talks.teaser: Explains ten common forms of cyber bullying, from exclusion and harassment to catfishing, to help parents recognise them.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Cyber-bullying is identified as a rapidly growing worldwide issue that directly affects children and their mental well-being. This presentation outlines the top ten common forms of cyber-bullying to equip parents with the necessary knowledge to identify these behaviors and protect their children.

### Key Topics & Forms of Cyber-Bullying
The presentation details ten specific manifestations of cyber-bullying:

1. **Exclusion**: Occurs when a child is deliberately left out of online activities, conversations, or social media tags. Children lacking the latest technology, such as mobile phones, are noted to be particularly prone to this form.
2. **Harassment**: Involves sustained, intentional bullying consisting of abusive or threatening messages directed at an individual child or a group, significantly impacting their mental health.
3. **Outing**: The act of publicly humiliating a child or group by sharing private or embarrassing information online without consent. This can also include actions such as reading a child's mobile phone messages out loud.
4. **Cyber Stalking**: A dangerous form of harassment executed through communications like email or social media. It also encompasses situations where adults use the internet to establish contact and arrange meetings with young individuals for abusive purposes.
5. **Fraping**: Happens when an unauthorized party accesses a child's social media account to impersonate them and post inappropriate content under their name. The transcript highlights that rude or inappropriate content posted online may never be fully eradicated, even after deletion.
6. **Fake Profiles**: Involves bullies creating deceptive accounts to mask their real identity while harassing a child, or utilizing someone else's email or mobile phone to send harassing messages.
7. **Dissing**: Spreading or posting cruel information, damaging photographs, screenshots, or videos online to tarnish a child's reputation or damage their relationships and friendships.
8. **Trickery**: The act of befriending a child to gain their trust and lure them into a false sense of security, solely to acquire secrets and subsequently share that private information publicly with others.
9. **Trolling**: Deliberately insulting and personally attacking a child on online forums or social media sites to provoke an angry response.
10. **Catfishing**: Stealing online identities to recreate social media profiles for deceptive purposes. Catfishers harvest information from a child's profile to build a fake persona, potentially jeopardizing the child's online reputation.

### Technical Details
While the talk does not cover deep-dive technical vulnerabilities or exploit code, it focuses on platforms and methods used by perpetrators, including compromised credentials/unauthorized access (fraping), identity spoofing and creation of fraudulent accounts (fake profiles, catfishing), communication channels (email, mobile messaging, social networks, forums), and digital persistence risks (content remaining online permanently despite deletion).

### Takeaways
- Parents must stay vigilant regarding the diverse digital tactics bullies use, ranging from passive exclusion to active harassment and social engineering (trickery).
- Online actions carry lasting consequences, as posted material can remain accessible indefinitely.
- Raising awareness among parents and sharing educational resources is essential to recognizing abuse early and putting an end to cyber-bullying.

talks.teaser: Traces how targeted attacks, ransomware and mobile threats have grown, and what that means for organizations.

The talk opens with an everyday scenario: an employee opens an attachment or clicks a link, and a zero-day exploit quietly installs malware that spreads across the network. The speakers argue that even a leading security firm can be hit this way, so the lesson is not to blame users. They then trace threats from early viruses and worms through spyware, phishing and botnets to advanced persistent threats, wipers and sabotage tools, noting that each new wave adds to the older ones rather than replacing them.

The speakers sort attackers into tiers, from low-end nuisance operators and financially motivated gangs up to a small top tier of nation-state groups, and they say the boundary between the top and the criminal tier is blurring. A bank intrusion case shows the pattern: criminals spent months inside a network, watched an administrator's work, then dispensed cash from ATMs remotely. Other topics include the dissolving network perimeter caused by personal devices and social media, mobile banking Trojans and spyware, and ransomware that victims often pay.

Looking ahead, they expect ransomware to keep growing, mobile and connected consumer devices to draw more attacks, and targeted operations to become quieter and more pragmatic. Small and medium businesses, which often lack IT or security staff, are presented as easy targets. The practical takeaway is that management and technical teams need to agree on priorities and accept some inconvenience, because attackers have time and money on their side.

talks.teaser: Argues that vulnerability disclosure policies keep failing because researchers and vendors lack trust in each other.

The talk examines why vulnerability disclosure keeps failing despite about fifteen years of competing policies from academics, vendor groups, and researchers. No single policy is widely adopted, because the ecosystem ranges from lone researchers to very large vendors in cars, medical devices, and startups. The speaker argues that the real gap is trust, which is slow to build, personal rather than organizational, and often damaged on both sides.

Examples show how this plays out. Public disclosure can speed a fix, yet it can hide a vendor's larger backlog of serious issues. A car maker that never gave researchers progress updates pushed them toward publishing, and a storage vendor's months-long runaround with an Australian researcher ended in a public dispute. Such cases teach researchers to see every vendor as unresponsive, while vendors see researchers as hostile.

The speaker's advice is practical. Companies should publish their disclosure policies and workflows so both sides have shared ground rules, mentor less mature vendors, and show trustworthy behavior. Listeners are urged to join the US government's multi-stakeholder disclosure working groups, which cover adoption, multi-vendor reporting, incentives, and safety for IoT and automotive.

talks.title: The need for security in transportation
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning The need for security in transportation.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Kurt Baumgartner, a principal security researcher with Kaspersky Lab's Global Research and Analysis Team (GReAT), discusses the growing cybersecurity risks within the transportation sector driven by the Internet of Things (IoT). Baumgartner explains that the rapid adoption of connected technologies across global logistics hubs, ports, and passenger vehicles is dramatically increasing attack surfaces while creating critical dependencies on potentially insecure systems.

### Key Topics
- **Maritime and Port Logistics:** Baumgartner highlights ports such as a facility in Latvia that handles 250,000 tons of hazardous chemical substances annually with a staff of only 10 people operating around the clock. He points out that this setup requires heavy reliance on management consoles, Wi-Fi, and online systems. Larger ports in Europe move around 200 million tons of cargo per year, while even larger facilities in India and Singapore similarly depend on small teams and interconnected digital infrastructure.
- **Automotive Surface and Connectivity:** With 250 million cars in the United States and growing vehicle counts in China, modern vehicles have become complex processing hubs. Modern cars feature around 60 different computer systems or CAN buses. The integration of cellular connections, Wi-Fi, telematics, satellite links, keyless entry, tire pressure monitoring, and ignition control exposes hundreds of millions of lines of code that were often developed without security as a primary design goal.
- **Public Hub and Consumer IoT Insecurities:** The speaker addresses vulnerabilities found across private consumer devices (refrigerators, coffee makers, TVs, baby monitors) and public infrastructure like CCTV and surveillance networks used in airports and shipping ports. Public implementations often suffer from plain text transmissions, disabled or missing WPA2, default administrative credentials, and unauthenticated debug ports.

### Technical Details
- **Automotive Exploits Timeline:** Baumgartner cites 2010 research from the University of Washington and University of California, San Diego, where researchers injected messages into a vehicle's CAN bus to achieve complete local control. He contrasts this with the 2015 research by Charlie Miller and Chris Valasek, who demonstrated remote car hacking that led to the recall of 1.4 million vehicles. This attack exploited the Sprint cellular network, which allowed cross-device communication between endpoints, permitting unauthorized access to exposed vehicle ports.
- **Satellite Abuse by Threat Actors:** Kaspersky's research identified APT groups actively exploiting unencrypted or vulnerable legacy satellite communications. Specifically, Baumgartner references the Turla APT and Poseidon APT groups abusing legacy satellite links that cannot be easily updated or patched.

### Takeaways
Baumgartner emphasizes that the transportation industry faces systemic cyber risks, noting that surveys of transportation organizations show nearly all have experienced internal or external security incidents. Vendor responses claiming that security issues will be addressed in the next hardware model fail to solve existing risks, particularly for legacy and critical infrastructure. Baumgartner calls for earlier security audits, penetration testing, and broader cross-industry collaboration before vulnerable systems are deployed.

talks.title: CATCHING CRYPTO-CRIMINALS: THAT WAS EASY!
talks.teaser: Traces how a ransomware case unfolded, from a victim's call to a free decryption tool and a joint police investigation.
talks.summary:
The talk follows the Coin Vault ransomware case from the moment a Swedish victim's files were locked to the investigation that followed. A compromised command-and-control server in the Netherlands was handed to the police, and the response was built around a four-step approach: help victims recover first, notify them, disrupt the criminals' business model, and only then pursue attribution. A victim website was set up, and a decryption tool was built quickly by reusing the decryption routine from the malware, which was written in .NET and was easy to decompile. A later infection led to a second command-and-control server and a full victim database.

The speaker then describes the malware's history. An earlier bot called Sonar logged keystrokes, searched for Bitcoin wallets, and collected FTP and email credentials before Coin Vault was delivered. An anti-analysis component checked for testing environments, and a leaked compile path exposed suspect names. Investigators combined police background checks, open-source research, forensic copies of servers and financial research into a case. When confronted, the suspects gave up the keys to an encrypted server holding backed-up decryption keys, which allowed those keys to be secured for victims.

The closing message is that solving cybercrime depends on everyone involved taking responsibility and on people being able to find each other and share information. The talk presents the case as proof that this kind of cooperation works in practice, even if it costs a few weekends.

talks.title: Hiding Traces High in the Skies
talks.teaser: Explains how the Turla group hides its command and control servers by abusing satellite internet traffic.
talks.summary:
This short video introduces satellite internet connections, which give access in places without high-speed lines. Their downlink traffic is unencrypted, so anyone within the broadcast footprint, which can span hundreds of miles, can intercept it. The Turla espionage group, a highly sophisticated malware platform, exploits this to conceal its command and control infrastructure.

The method works in stages. The attackers first listen to the satellite's downstream traffic to collect the IP addresses of users online. They then instruct computers already infected with Turla malware to send stolen data to servers the group chooses. Those servers pose as the address of the legitimate subscriber, so both the attackers and the real user receive packets from the infected machines. The traffic is aimed at ports that are normally closed, but the attackers keep them open, so the victim notices nothing. Because the operators can sit anywhere inside the satellite's coverage area, tracing the real server becomes very difficult for investigators.

The key takeaway is that discovering the server's location would expose the operation at both ends, which is why the group values this anonymity so highly. The video closes by noting that Kaspersky products can detect and block the malware used by this threat actor.

The talk examines SecureDrop, an open-source whistleblower submission system maintained by the Freedom of the Press Foundation. The speaker explains that encryption cannot protect a source whose device is already compromised, so SecureDrop assumes a clean Tor browser and the genuine onion address. About fifteen media organizations, mostly in the United States, run it as Tor hidden services.

Sources land on a newsroom's page, receive a generated code name and can optionally encrypt files to a journalist's public key before uploading. Journalists use a separate authenticated hidden service that needs a Tor configuration token, a password and a two-factor code, and sources appear under two-word code names. The servers sit in the newsroom, and documents are viewed on an air-gapped Tails machine carried over by USB, with replies sent back from a networked Tor setup.

The closing section looks at adoption. The speaker argues that sources rarely see themselves as sources, that journalists need training to handle sensitive material, and that newsrooms struggle to commit time to regular practice. Questions covered document verification and legal pressure, and the speaker knew of no legal issues so far. The takeaway is that the tool solves one narrow problem and the surrounding human workflow matters just as much.

talks.title: OpSec for security researchers
talks.teaser: Offers practical, non-technical advice for security researchers facing surveillance, recruitment attempts and border device searches.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that most operational security advice is unrealistic because it focuses on tools and techniques instead of how people should act in real situations. The speakers treat OPSEC as a matter of discipline, preparation and awareness. They focus on state agencies as the most capable adversaries a researcher is likely to meet, while noting that smaller groups can also be dangerous. Mass surveillance makes encryption essential, but data encrypted today may be decrypted later if passwords or keys are obtained through physical or coercive means.

Next come scenarios researchers may face. If a person is profiled and approached through proxies with money, flattery or suggestions of being overlooked, the advice is to refuse and redirect the request to a better-prepared colleague. Before a suspicious meeting, the speakers recommend not going alone, not using the other side's transport, scouting safe public places or an embassy, and agreeing a check-in with a colleague as a dead man switch. They also warn that a meeting may be a trap to get a laptop left behind. At borders, they say legal exceptions often allow device searches without a warrant, so travellers should not obstruct or lie, and should carry no sensitive data, or use encrypted or anti-coercion options if they must.

The common thread is reliance on external help: an employer's international support contact, a country briefing suited to researchers, and personal homework before travel. The speakers stress staying calm, not playing a role you are not suited for, and keeping people informed.

talks.title: Tools of NSA playset
talks.teaser: Surveys low-cost hardware implants and attack tools, from I2C and USB taps to PCIe DMA devices hidden in cables.
talks.summary:
Joe Fitzpatrick, a hardware security researcher and trainer, introduces the "NSA playset," a collection of hobbyist recreations of tools listed in a leaked NSA ANT catalog. His premise is that many of the catalog's capabilities can be built from off-the-shelf parts and open-source software for a small fraction of the quoted prices, so defenders should not treat them as out of reach.

He walks through the devices in the set. These include a passive radio-reflecting listening bug, a bootable USB environment for GSM monitoring that pairs with a cheap TV tuner and a rainbow-table drive, and a Bluetooth kit that can take over an existing keyboard pairing. He also covers an I2C implant that uses the monitor's display bus to move data, a USB cable with a built-in radio that can store and transmit traffic, and a USB man-in-the-middle board. His own project, Slot Screamer, is a PCI Express attack platform that connects over USB and issues arbitrary memory reads and writes. He shows it packaged in a Thunderbolt enclosure, an ExpressCard version, and a cable disguised as a VGA cable for presentation rooms.

He closes by arguing that designers should scope protections against cheap DIY tools, not only nation-state capabilities. He notes that Apple has hardened Thunderbolt against this class of attack, while a standard Linux install often leaves bus mastering enabled on every PCIe device. The takeaway is that DMA exposure and unmonitored hardware buses belong in threat models.

talks.title: How I hacked my home
talks.teaser: Follows a security researcher who finds root-level flaws in the everyday connected devices in his own home.
talks.summary:
David, a senior security researcher at Kaspersky, argues that the security industry spends its attention on exotic threats such as car hacking and rarely addresses the connected devices people actually own. To test this, he examined the gear in his newly bought house, which included a network storage device, a smart TV, Blu-ray and DVD players, a network printer, and some vintage computers, and he looked at how much of it could be attacked.

On the network storage device, he reached remote code execution as root in about twenty minutes, even though the device required a login. A configuration file, holding password hashes, was readable in clear text by anyone without authentication, so protecting shares with a username and password meant little. The root flaw came from user input being passed straight into a system command. Across two storage devices he counted 22 vulnerabilities. He then demonstrated a drive-by attack: a crafted web page reached root on the storage device through a single link, and a later version scanned the local network in the background so that visiting the page required no clicks at all. He noted the same approach could work from a phone, tablet or TV. The TV ran an outdated Apache and a very old Linux kernel, and he described a router with hidden administrative features. After he tampered with the router, the provider locked him out and sent a bill.

The takeaway is that consumer products often receive support for only about six months, so flaws in them tend to stay unpatched. Most homes also lack network segmentation, which lets one weak gadget reach everything else. When he reported the flaws, the vendors gave only generic thanks. He argues the industry should discuss these simple, relevant problems as much as headline-grabbing research.

talks.title: Security lessons from the Sochi Olympics
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Security lessons from the Sochi Olympics.
talks.summary:
Overview
This talk covers security operations and incident response during the Sochi Olympic Games. The security team managed up to 70 incidents daily while retrofitting security measures into infrastructure that was not originally designed with security in mind. Despite the high incident volume, no breaches were publicly announced.

Key Challenge: The Journalist Factor
The speaker emphasizes that 13,000 journalists attending the games created an unexpected security variable. These journalists had built automated monitoring systems for the Olympic infrastructure and could publish articles about security issues within minutes of their occurrence. A DDoS attack lasting only three minutes resulted in article publication within two minutes of the attack start.

Four Major Incidents

1. FTP Server Breach (New Year's Eve): Stolen FTP accounts were being sold for $10,000 per account on hacking forums. The compromised server had improper configuration and direct access to the domain controller. Analysis revealed Wireshark installation, deleted logs, and 50+ compromised accounts including administrative and security officer accounts.

2. Undetected Brazilian Bank Trojan: Using AVZ malware detection technology (which automatically processes logs and quarantines), the team discovered specially crafted malware initially undetected by any antivirus. The same malware appeared in modified form two months later and again one month after that. Analysis revealed it targeted the finance department, stealing banking client accounts, AD credentials, and VPN accounts.

3. Botnet Discovery: During forensics work for another customer, the team found references to Olympic infrastructure IP addresses in botnet configuration files. This led to discovery of three additional botnets, with detailed analysis showing significant data theft and account compromises.

4. Insider Threat (4 AM Incident): A first-line network engineer was discovered conducting suspicious activities including disk wiping tools, cryptography tools, malware tools (Metasploit), and antivirus evasion attempts. Investigation revealed he was a previously convicted attacker (multiple federal website attacks) who had gained employment using false identity and was preparing a serious attack on critical Olympic resources.

Defensive Measures and Results
The team deployed multiple APT detection services, cyber intelligence platforms, and AVZ-based automated malware analysis. Overall statistics: 100,000+ malware attacks prevented (primarily trojans and Java exploits) and 2,000+ attacks detected on honeypot systems.

Lessons Learned
- Secure by design: integrate security from inception, not retrofit
- Invest in quality people and best-in-class tools (Kaspersky Lab technology)
- Customer education and building client confidence in expertise is essential

talks.title: The challenges of detecting silent exits of your data
talks.teaser: Explains why data leaving a large network is hard to spot and how a bank approaches egress monitoring and risk management.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a party story about a guest who leaves unnoticed, a "silent exit," which the speaker uses to describe data leaving a network without anyone seeing it. He argues that large organizations with hundreds of thousands of endpoints, many third-party suppliers, and cloud services that business units can buy with a credit card cannot track every outbound flow. Attackers have moved from disrupting front doors to taking information, and the traditional perimeter no longer holds.

He uses the Anthem breach to show why stolen personal data is valuable for impersonation, and says insider threats and compromised third parties deserve equal attention. He then compares disclosure timelines: after one SSL flaw, public exploit code appeared within about 48 hours, and a second bug was followed by destructive malware within hours. Many organizations do not know where a vulnerable library is used, which slows their response.

His practical advice is to build a risk management framework that classifies data and defines what may leave the network, encrypt sensitive data inside the network, and baseline the outbound data the business needs so anomalies stand out. Each new technology should have a contingency plan, and threat intelligence helps teams understand attacker tradecraft. The takeaway is to assume someone is already inside, accept that tools will miss some things, and invest in people and process alongside technology.

talks.title: Eugene Kaspersky discusses the Stuxnet virus on Cybercrimes
talks.teaser: Traces the discovery, design and suspected geopolitical origins of the Stuxnet worm and what it means for future cyber conflict.
talks.summary:
This BBC documentary opens with fears that a cyber weapon could disrupt power grids, trains and financial systems, then follows the 2010 discovery of Stuxnet. A security firm was first alerted by an Iranian client whose computers kept freezing and rebooting. Researchers later found that the worm used several zero-day flaws and two stolen digital certificates, and that it targeted programmable logic controllers used in industrial processes, especially uranium enrichment.

The program describes how the worm reached centrifuges at the Natanz plant. It changed their spin speeds, which could break them, while feeding operators normal readings. The documentary also covers Operation Orchard, a 2007 Israeli strike on a Syrian nuclear site, where air defense radars were reportedly disabled through cyber means before the bombs fell. It reports that the United States and Israel have been linked to Stuxnet in press accounts, though neither government has confirmed involvement. Interviewed experts stress how hard such attacks are to attribute, and how a cyber attack on a grid could cascade across regions.

The program then weighs whether cyber war is overstated, since no major attack has yet destroyed physical infrastructure. It suggests that a USB drive was the likely route past the air gap that isolated the plant's computers, and it cites a government experiment in which most drives left in parking lots were plugged into office machines. The closing point is that human motives still drive conflict, and that the Stuxnet code was quickly copied after discovery. The practical lessons are to treat removable media as a real threat to isolated networks and to recognize that attribution of state-level cyber attacks remains difficult.

This short clip argues that smartphones, tablets, laptops and PCs with webcams are connected devices that malicious software can take over, including their cameras. Beyond reading private images, an attacker could take pictures of the victim without their knowledge. The speaker contrasts how people guard their homes and avoid dark alleys with how casually they treat their digital lives.

The talk leans on survey figures to make the point. Eighty-three percent of respondents never turn their phones off unless the battery runs out, and 96 percent keep them within reach at all times. Around four in ten take them into the toilet, a third get undressed in their presence, and more than half say they have had sex within sight of a camera-enabled device. A baby monitor case, in which an unknown person spoke to a ten-month-old through a hacked connected device, is cited as an example of how such intrusions happen.

The risk also reaches backwards and into everyday habits. Images stored on a device, from student parties to baby videos, could be exposed. The speaker warns that holding a payment card up to the camera while typing its number into a website could let someone who has hijacked the camera capture those details. The closing message is that people should secure connected devices with the same care they give to locking their front door.

talks.title: Tor and the Average Internet User, Runa Sandvick, Tor Project advocate
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Tor and the Average Internet User, Runa Sandvick, Tor Project advocate.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk excerpt, the speaker discusses the practical importance of Tor for everyday internet users, beyond just specialized groups like journalists and human rights activists. The presentation highlights how Tor allows individuals to regain control of their online privacy by concealing web browsing activities from local observers and websites alike, while also serving as a tool for censorship circumvention.

### Key Topics
- **Online Privacy for Normal Users**: How everyday users can use Tor to ensure their internet service provider (ISP), employers, or shared computer users cannot monitor which websites they visit, and prevent websites from knowing who is visiting them.
- **The "Anonymity Loves Company" Principle**: Tor relies on a broad and diverse user base. When average users adopt Tor, it directly strengthens anonymity and security for high-risk users, such as human rights activists and journalists who depend on the network.
- **Censorship Circumvention**: Tor provides the ability to bypass network restrictions or national censorship when specific websites are blocked.
- **Data Profiling and Tracking**: Commercial entities collect and analyze online activities to build behavioral profiles, often deducing personal information without explicit disclosure.

### Technical Details
*(Note: The provided transcript excerpt contains limited technical detail regarding the underlying Tor architecture or protocol implementations.)*
- Tor obscures traffic bidirectionally: ISPs and local network observers cannot see the destination websites, and destination websites cannot identify the originating visitor.
- Data aggregation is contrasted against Tor's privacy guarantees: corporate tracking analyzes patterns in online behavior and shopping habits to deduce sensitive private details, illustrated by an example of Target identifying a teenage customer's pregnancy through shifts in product purchasing habits.

### Takeaways
- Tor is not only for high-profile or high-risk individuals; everyday users benefit directly by shielding their online habits from recording, analysis, and profiling.
- Widespread adoption of Tor by ordinary internet users is vital to the entire anonymity ecosystem, providing safety in numbers for everyone using the system.
- Tor serves both privacy protection and access enablement by bypassing local network and geographic website blocks.

talks.title: Future Trend of Advanced Persistent Threats (APT) Video | Hear the expert insights
talks.teaser: Surveys emerging trends in advanced persistent threat groups, from cheaper entry and supply chain targeting to destructive attacks.
talks.summary:
Kurt Baumgartner outlines how advanced persistent threat groups are changing and what enterprises should expect next. The main shift he describes is that the cost of entry for attackers is falling while their activity grows more precise and frequent. He points to cyber mercenary groups that arrive with a specific goal inside an organization, take what they need, cover their tracks and move on. Sharing knowledge about actors also gets harder when work is spread across contractors and subcontractors in different countries, since those parties rarely compare notes on activity that crosses borders.

He then covers the growing overlap between commercial and government targets and the use of supply chains as a route to a larger prize. Rather than attacking a well-defended parent company, attackers go after smaller subcontractors that serve as a launching pad. He gives the example of a retailer whose contractors were compromised, letting intruders move deeper into the retailer and steal customer payment card data. He also describes a rise in destructive activity, including wiper attacks that delete data and disable systems across large numbers of machines, and prolonged DDoS campaigns that take web servers offline to make a political statement or damage a target directly.

For practitioners, the message is to map which partners and subcontractors can reach their systems, and to prepare for disruptive and availability attacks as well as data theft.

Kurt Baumgartner of Kaspersky Lab introduces Careto, also called The Mask, as a highly advanced threat actor. He describes it as unusual: it ran a relatively small number of victims across significant campaigns, and it kept tight control over both its development and its operations.

The group built boot kits and rootkits able to capture Wi-Fi communications and PGP keys, along with other ways of encrypting and hiding sensitive data. Its targets ranged from government organizations to private equity firms and energy companies, and it went after Windows, Apple and Linux systems alike. Its most notable trait was attacking the defenses themselves. It exploited older flaws in antivirus and anti-malware products to reach its victims, something earlier actors such as Duqu and Flame had not done. When exposed, it shut down its infrastructure more effectively than Red October or Flame had.

Baumgartner argues that the group is likely a nation-state-backed operation and will not simply go away once discovered. His practical takeaway is that defenders must understand the adversary, and understand their own network well enough to defend it and shake such an actor off.

talks.title: Facebook Privacy Settings Advice Video
talks.teaser: Walks through Facebook's privacy and timeline settings and explains which options to tighten for less public exposure.
talks.summary:
This video is a follow-up to an earlier segment on Facebook security and focuses on privacy. It opens by noting that deactivating an account is the most private option, then explains that people who need to keep an account can download a copy of the data Facebook holds about them. The presenter's stated goal is a high level of privacy without becoming antisocial.

Moving through the privacy settings, the presenter recommends limiting future posts to friends or to only the user, and suggests reviewing the friend list regularly and removing contacts who post spam or whom the user no longer recognises. Posts can be audited and changed in bulk so that old content is visible only to friends. Friend requests are best restricted to friends of friends, and rejecting unknown requests is encouraged. Message filtering should be set to strict. Lookup by email address and phone number should be limited to friends, and the option that lets outside search engines link to the timeline should be turned off.

The timeline and tagging section covers who can post on the timeline, reviewing tags before they appear, and who can see posts the user is tagged in. The presenter also suggests reviewing tags added to one's own posts and restricting facial-recognition tag suggestions to no one. The video closes by recommending privacy and security notifications and pointing viewers to the earlier security video. The main takeaway is that default settings often expose more than users expect, so each section is worth checking.

The final section turns to critical infrastructure, such as water and electricity supply, where a failure would have serious consequences for organizations and nations. The speaker notes that many of these systems were built in the 1960s and 1970s without considering today's threat landscape, so organizations and governments need to revisit that technology to protect themselves and surrounding countries from current cyber threats.

This short interview, recorded at Mobile World Congress in Barcelona, features a senior analyst from Kaspersky Lab discussing how mobile technology is changing the threat landscape. The analyst argues that the growing number of connected devices widens the attack surface, and that new mobile payment systems give fraudsters fresh opportunities.

On mobile banking, the analyst says phones carry the same weaknesses as computers, and many users do not realise a handset can be infected. Banking once split the work between a computer for transfers and an SMS code on a phone for confirmation. Now both steps happen on one device, so an attacker who controls the phone gets access to everything. The recommended defence is many layers: an SDK inside banking apps, behavioural analysis, and clientless monitoring of user actions. This helps banks detect fraud while also protecting the customer's device.

Looking ahead, the analyst expects ransomware to move from PCs to phones. Connected devices such as cars and home systems are seen as the next area of collateral damage, with targeted attacks likely to follow. On biometrics such as fingerprints and face scans, the analyst sees a real improvement over passwords but flags privacy concerns about storing biometric data online, and suggests pairing it with another factor. The debate is presented as unfinished but a positive step.
